## A Closer Look at Critical Regions and p-values ** {#sec-closer-look-cr-pvalue}

::: {.callout-note}
This section is optional. The material here is not required for performing hypothesis tests, but it is highly recommended for readers who want a firmer conceptual grasp of what is happening behind the procedures.
:::


In the previous sections, you learned two equivalent approaches for testing a hypothesis about a population proportion: the **critical region approach** and the **p-value approach**. In both approaches, we computed probabilities for our decisions using the boundary value of the null hypothesis, and we relied on Rguroo's [Proportion Infrence]{.fun} function to produce the critical region or the p-value automatically.

This section is intended to deepen your understanding of *why* these procedures work the way they do. Specifically, we address two questions:

1. **Why do we use the boundary value of $H_0$ when computing probabilities required for our decisions?** The null hypothesis in many tests is a statement such as $H_0: p \leq p_0$ or $H_0: p \geq p_0$, which encompasses many possible values of $p$. Yet we always use the single boundary value $p_0$ in our calculations. There is a principled reason for this, and understanding it clarifies what a hypothesis test is really doing.

2. **How are critical regions and p-values actually obtained from a probability distribution?** Rguroo's [Proportion Inference]{.fun} function returns these quantities directly, but doing so hides the underlying probability calculation. By using Rguroo's **probability calculator** instead, we can see exactly which area under a sampling distribution corresponds to the critical region or the p-value. 


### Why Use the Boundary Value in $H_0$? ** {#sec-boundary-value}

In this section we explain *why* we use the boundary value of $H_0$ when computing the probability of a Type I error. The front-half discussion stated this as a fact: for a composite $H_0$ such as $H_0: p \leq p_0$, the maximum Type I error probability over the values allowed by $H_0$ occurs at the boundary $p_0$, so controlling the error there automatically controls it everywhere in $H_0$. Here we *demonstrate* this empirically: we compute the probability of a Type I error for several specific values of $p$ within $H_0$, for one decision rule, and observe that the maximum occurs at the boundary. A formal account, including worked examples and the underlying mathematics, is given in [Jamshidian and Jamshidian (2026)](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/26939169.2025.2610942).


:::{#exm-youtube-type1}
## Daily YouTube Use Among Teens (continued)

Recall @exm-youtube-ppss where a school district claimed that more than 70% of 
students in its district use YouTube daily, and a random sample of $n = 20$ 
students was selected. The null and alternative hypotheses are:
$$
\begin{cases}
H_0: p \leq 0.70 \\
H_a: p > 0.70
\end{cases}
$$

Consider the critical region: Reject $H_0$ if $X \geq 17$.

For this critical region, compute $P(\text{Type I error})$ when 

a. $p = 0.60$
b. $p = 0.65$
c. $p = 0.70$.

In each case, interpret the probability in the context of the problem.
:::

:::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution
a\. Since the sample size is $n = 20$ and $p = 0.60$, we have 
$X \sim \text{Binomial}(20, 0.60)$. Using Rguroo's probability calculator, 
we compute
$$P(\text{Type I error}) = P(\text{Reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ is true})$$
$$= P(X \geq 17 \mid p = 0.60).$$

Click to expand the box below to see how to calculate the probability of Type I error.

:::{#calculating-typeI-error .callout-note appearance="simple" 
collapse="true" icon="none" 
title="![](Rguroo_Icons/R_circle_logo.svg){width=22px 
style='vertical-align:middle;'} Calculating Type I Error Probability"}

1. Open the **Probability-Simulation** toolbox in Rguroo.  
2. From the [Probability]{.dpd} dropdown, select 
[Probability Calculator --> Discrete]{.fun}.
3. (Optional) In the `Calculation` textbox, type a name for the calculation 
(e.g., `Type I error`).  
4. In the [Distribution]{.dpd} dropdown, select [Binomial]{.fun}.
5. In the [No. of Trials]{.des} textbox, enter [20]{.typein}.
6. In the [Prob. of Success]{.des} textbox, enter [0.60]{.typein}.
7. In the next dropdown menu, select [Above]{.dpd}, and in the textbox next 
to it, enter [17]{.typein}.
8. (Optional) Select the [Graph]{.des} checkbox to see a graph showing 
calculation details.
9. Click the preview icon ![preview icon](Rguroo_Icons/preview_inline.png) 
to see the result.
10. (Optional) In the ![Save as](Rguroo_Icons/save_as.png) textbox, enter 
the name [TypeI_Error]{.typein} to save this calculation to your Rguroo 
account.

::: {.callout-tip .inner-callout appearance="simple" collapse="true" 
icon="none" title="Click here to see the Rguroo dialog"}
![Probability calculator dialog for computing Type I error probability
](Rguroo_dialogs/Proportion_inference/Prob_Type_I_error_dialog.png){width=500px}
:::

::::

@fig-youtube-type1a shows the Rguroo Probability Calculator output for 
$X \sim \text{Binomial}(20, 0.60)$, giving 

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
$$P(\text{Type I error}) = P(X \geq 17\mid p=0.60) \approx 0.016.$$
:::

That is, if the true proportion of students in the district who use YouTube 
daily is $p = 0.60$, and our decision rule is to reject $H_0$ whenever 
$X \geq 17$ in a sample of $n = 20$ students, then there is only a $1.6\%$ 
chance of committing a Type I error; that is, incorrectly concluding that 
more than 70% of students in the district use YouTube daily.
```{r,echo=FALSE}
#| fig-cap: "Binomial distribution for $X \\sim \\text{Binomial}(n = 20, p = 0.60)$ showing the Type I error probability as the upper-tail area $P(X \\geq 17) = 0.016$."
#| warning: FALSE
#| label: fig-youtube-type1a
#| out-width: "80%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/Prob_Type_I_Error_graph.png")
```

b\. To compute the probability of Type I error for the critical region 
$X \geq 17$ when $p = 0.65$, we follow the same steps as in 
the [part (a)](#calculating-typeI-error), but enter [0.65]{.typein} in the 
[Prob. of Success]{.des} box. The Rguroo output gives 

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
$$P(\text{Type I error}) = P(X \geq 17\mid p=0.65) \approx 0.044.$$
:::

That is, if the true proportion of students in the district who use YouTube 
daily is $p = 0.65$, and our decision rule is to reject $H_0$ whenever 
$X \geq 17$ in a sample of $n = 20$ students, then there is approximately a 
$4.4\%$ chance of committing a Type I error; that is, incorrectly concluding 
that more than 70% of students in the district use YouTube daily.

c\. Entering [0.70]{.typein} in the [Prob. of Success]{.des} box gives

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
$$P(\text{Type I error}) = P(X \geq 17\mid p=0.70) \approx 0.107.$$
:::

That is, if the true proportion of students in the district who use YouTube 
daily is $p = 0.70$, and our decision rule is to reject $H_0$ whenever 
$X \geq 17$ in a sample of $n = 20$ students, then there is approximately a 
$10.7\%$ chance of committing a Type I error; that is, incorrectly concluding 
that more than 70% of students in the district use YouTube daily.
:::

:::{#exm-physical-inactivity-type1}
## Physical Inactivity Among Adults (continued)

Recall @exm-physical-inactivity-ppss where a national health agency claimed 
that fewer than 35% of adults in its country are physically inactive, and a 
random sample of $n = 50$ adults was selected. The null and alternative 
hypotheses are:
$$
\begin{cases}
H_0: p \geq 0.35 \\
H_a: p < 0.35
\end{cases}
$$

Consider the critical region: Reject $H_0$ if $X \leq 13$.

For this critical region, compute $P(\text{Type I error})$ when 

a. $p = 0.35$ 
b. $p = 0.40$
c. $p = 0.50$.

In each case, interpret the probability in the context of the problem.
:::

:::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution

a\. Since the sample size is $n = 50$ and $p = 0.35$, we have 
$X \sim \text{Binomial}(50, 0.35)$. Using Rguroo's probability calculator, 
we compute
$$P(\text{Type I error}) = P(\text{Reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ is true})$$
$$= P(X \leq 13 \mid p = 0.35).$$

Use the same Rguroo Probability Calculator steps as in the [YouTube example](#calculating-typeI-error), with [No. of Trials]{.des} = 50, [Prob. of Success]{.des} = 0.35, and the direction set to [Below]{.dpd} with value 13:

::: {.callout-tip .inner-callout appearance="simple" collapse="true" 
icon="none" title="Click here to see the Rguroo dialog"}
![Probability calculator dialog for computing Type I error probability
](Rguroo_dialogs/Proportion_inference/TypeI_Error_Inactivity_dialog.png){width=500px}
:::


@fig-inactivity-type1 shows the Rguroo Probability Calculator output for 
$X \sim \text{Binomial}(50, 0.35)$, giving 

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
$$P(\text{Type I error}) = P(X \leq 13\mid p=0.35) \approx 0.1163.$$
:::

That is, if the true proportion of inactive adults in the population is 
$p = 0.35$, and our decision rule is to reject $H_0$ whenever $X \leq 13$ 
in a sample of $n = 50$ adults, then there is approximately an $11.63\%$ chance 
of committing a Type I error; that is, incorrectly concluding that fewer than 
35% of adults in the population are physically inactive.
```{r,echo=FALSE}
#| fig-cap: "Binomial distribution for $X \\sim \\text{Binomial}(n = 50, p = 0.35)$ showing the Type I error probability as the lower-tail area $P(X \\leq 13) = 0.1163$."
#| warning: FALSE
#| label: fig-inactivity-type1
#| out-width: "80%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/Type I Error Inactivity_graph.png")
```

\ 

b\. Entering [0.40]{.typein} in the [Prob. of Success]{.des} box gives

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
$$P(\text{Type I error}) = P(X \leq 13\mid p=0.40) \approx 0.028.$$
:::

That is, if the true proportion of inactive adults in the population is 
$p = 0.40$, and our decision rule is to reject $H_0$ whenever $X \leq 13$ 
in a sample of $n = 50$ adults, then there is approximately a $2.8\%$ chance 
of committing a Type I error; that is, incorrectly concluding that fewer than 
35% of adults in the population are physically inactive.

c\. Entering [0.50]{.typein} in the [Prob. of Success]{.des} box gives

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
$$P(\text{Type I error}) = P(X \leq 13\mid p=0.50) \approx 0.00046.$$
:::

That is, if the true proportion of inactive adults in the population is 
$p = 0.50$, and our decision rule is to reject $H_0$ whenever $X \leq 13$ 
in a sample of $n = 50$ adults, then there is approximately a $0.046\%$ chance 
of committing a Type I error; that is, incorrectly concluding that fewer than 
35% of adults in the population are physically inactive.

::::

Now that we have computed the probability of a Type I error at various values 
of $p$, let us look back at what we observed in our examples. 

For the one-sided cases,  there is a range of values of $p$ in
$H_0$, and we computed the probability of a Type I error at several of them. 
You may have noticed a pattern: in both the YouTube example and the Physical 
Inactivity example, the probability of a Type I error was largest at the value 
of $p$ where $H_0$ and $H_a$ meet, the **boundary value of $p$ in $H_0$**. 
For the YouTube example, this is $p = 0.70$, and for the Physical Inactivity example, this is $p = 0.35$. Is this a coincidence that the probability of a Type I error is largest at the boundary value? 

The answer is, it is not a coincident. @fig-type-range shows the probability of a Type I error across a range of values of $p$ in $H_0$, 
for the two examples that we considerd here and for three different decision rules in each case.

```{r,echo=FALSE}
#| fig-cap: 'Type I error probabilities for binomial tests as a function of $p$. Panel (a) shows $X \sim \text{Binomial}(20, p)$ with $P(X \geq 16, 17, 18)$; panel (b) shows $X \sim \text{Binomial}(50, p)$ with $P(X \leq 11, 12, 13)$. The red dashed line marks $\alpha = 0.05$. The gray dotted line shows the boundary of $H_0$.'
#| fig-alt: 'Two side-by-side line graphs showing how Type I error changes with the true proportion π. In panel (a), for a binomial model with n = 20, three curves show P(X ≥ 16), P(X ≥ 17), and P(X ≥ 18) increasing as p increases from 0 to 0.70, with values up to about 0.25. In panel (b), for n = 50, three curves show P(X ≤ 11), P(X ≤ 12), and P(X ≤ 13) decreasing as π increases from 0.35 to 1, with values up to about 0.12. A horizontal red dashed line at 0.05 marks the significance level in both plots.'
#| warning: FALSE
#| label: fig-type-range
#| out-width: "90%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/TypeI_error_range.png")
```

In panel (a), for the YouTube example, the null hypothesis is 
$H_0: p \leq 0.70$, so the boundary value is $p = 0.70$. The three curves 
correspond to the decision rules $X \geq 16$, $X \geq 17$, and $X \geq 18$. 
For all three rules, the probability of a Type I error increases as $p$ gets 
closer to the boundary value of $0.70$, and reaches its maximum at $p = 0.70$. 

In panel (b), for the Physical Inactivity example, the null hypothesis is 
$H_0: p \geq 0.35$, so the boundary value is $p = 0.35$. The three curves 
correspond to the decision rules $X \leq 11$, $X \leq 12$, and $X \leq 13$. 
Again, for all three rules, the probability of a Type I error is largest at the 
boundary value $p = 0.35$ and decreases as $p$ moves away from it. 

::: {.callout-note}
## Key Result: Maximum Type I Error Occurs at the Boundary Value
For the one-sided tests, the probability of a Type I error is largest at the boundary value of $H_0$.
:::

Notice also that the horizontal dashed red line in each panel is drawn at $0.05$. This represents a commonly chosen upper bound for the probability of a Type I error — that is, the significance level $\alpha = 0.05$. As discussed in the previous sections, the decision rule (critical region) that we use is chosen to satisfy two requirements:

1. At the boundary value of $H_0$, the probability of a Type I error does not exceed the desired significance level $\alpha$.
2. Among all critical regions satisfying (1), we choose the one containing the largest number of $X$ values, so that the probability of a Type II error is as small as possible.

Therefore, as shown in @fig-type-range, the critical region corresponding to the significance level $\alpha = 0.05$ for the YouTube example is $X\geq 18$, and that for the Physical Inactivity example is $X\leq 11$.


### Obtaining Critical Regions and p-values Using Rguroo's Probability Calculator{#sec-prob-calculator}

In this subsection, we revisit examples from earlier in the chapter, but instead of using Rguroo's [Proportion Inference]{.fun} function, we compute critical values and p-values directly from the sampling distribution under $H_0$ using Rguroo's [Probability Calculator]{.fun} function. This approach makes visible the area-under-the-curve interpretation of both quantities.

#### Using Inverse Probability to Find the Critical Region

When using a probability calculator, we could find a critical region by trying different candidate decision rules and checking their Type I error probabilities one at a time, as illustrated in @fig-type-range. For example, we might check whether the rule "$X \ge 17$” has a Type I error probability close to 0.05, then try “$X \ge 18$,” and so on. While this trial-and-error approach works, there is a more direct method.

Many calculators provide an inverse probability function. A probability function starts with a value of $X$ and returns the corresponding probability. An inverse probability function works in the opposite direction: we provide a probability, such as $\alpha=0.05$, and it returns the value of $X$ that creates that probability. This allows us to find the rejection-region boundary directly rather than testing several possible decision rules one at a time.

To find the critical region, we use the binomial distribution with the boundary value of $p$ from $H_0$ as the probability of success and $n$ as the number of trials. Instead of providing a value of $X$ and asking for a probability, we provide the significance level $\alpha$ as the probability. The inverse probability function then returns the corresponding boundary value of $X$, which we use to determine the critical region. Below, we show how this is done in Rguroo using its built-in probability calculator.

::: {#exm-youtube-rejection-calc}
## YouTube Use: Finding the Critical Region

In the YouTube Use example (@exm-youtube-ppss), we are testing 
$H_0: p \leq 0.70$ versus $H_a: p > 0.70$, where $p$ is the true 
proportion of students in the district who use YouTube daily. Using a sample of $n = 20$ students and a significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$, find the critical region for this test.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution
Since the alternative hypothesis is $H_a: p > 0.70$, large values of $X$ provide evidence in favor of $H_a$. Therefore, we need a critical region in the upper tail of the binomial distribution. We use Rguroo’s [Probability Calculator]{.fun} and the significance level $\alpha$ to find the boundary value of $X$ that defines this region.

Click to expand the box below to see how to use the [Probability Calulator]{.fun} function in Rguroo.

::: {#probability-youtube .callout-note appearance="simple" collapse="true" icon="none" title="![](Rguroo_Icons/R_circle_logo.svg){width=22px style='vertical-align:middle;'} Critical Region Using Calculator — YouTube example"}

1.  Open the **Probability-Simulation** toolbox

2. Select [Probability $\Rightarrow$ Values]{.des} to use the inverse probability function.

3. In the [Distribution]{.dpd} dropdown, set the distribution to _Binomial_.

4. Set the [No. of Trials]{.des} to [20]{.typein} and the [Prob. of Success]{.des} 
to [0.70]{.typein}.

5. From the dropdown, select [Upper Tail]{.dpd} and enter [$0.05$]{.typein} as the significance level $\alpha$.

6. Select the checkbox [Graph]{.des} to see a detailed output.

::: {.callout-tip .inner-callout collapse="true" title="Rguroo Discrete Probability Calculator  dialog"}


```{r,echo=FALSE}
#| fig-alt: "Rguroo Discrete Distributions Probability Calculator configured for the YouTube example with Binomial distribution, 20 trials, probability of success 0.70, upper tail selected, and significance level 0.05 entered."
#| warning: FALSE
#| label: fig-youtube-rejection-dialog
#| fig-cap: "Rguroo Probability Calculator Settings for the YouTube Critical Region Example"
#| out-width: "90%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_dialogs/Proportion_inference/youtube-rejection-dialog.png")
```
:::

:::

The output, shown in @fig-youtube-rejection, gives
$$
P(X \geq 17)=0.1071 > 0.05
\quad\text{and}\quad
P(X \geq 18)=0.03548 < 0.05.
$$
```{r,echo=FALSE}
#| fig-alt: "Binomial distribution histogram for n = 20 and p = 0.70, with the critical region X greater than or equal to 18 highlighted in gold, showing that P(X greater than or equal to 17) = 0.1071 exceeds 0.05 and P(X greater than or equal to 18) = 0.03548 does not."
#| warning: FALSE
#| label: fig-youtube-rejection
#| fig-cap: "Rguroo Probability Calculator Output for the YouTube Critical Region Example"
#| out-width: "80%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/YouTube_rejection.png")
```

Thus, the decision rule $X \geq 17$ would produce a Type I error probability greater than our significance level and cannot be used. However, the decision rule $X \geq 18$ has a Type I error probability below 0.05 and therefore satisfies the significance-level requirement.

Therefore, the critical region at significance level $\alpha=0.05$ is
$$
X \geq 18.
$$
In other words, if 18 or more of the $n=20$ students in the sample report daily YouTube use, we reject $H_0$ in favor of $H_a: p>0.70$.

:::


::: {#exm-inactivity-rejection-calc}
## Physical Inactivity: Finding the Critical Region

In the Physical Inactivity example (@exm-physical-inactivity-error), we are 
testing $H_0: p \geq 0.35$ versus $H_a: p < 0.35$, where $p$ is the 
true proportion of adults in the population who are physically inactive. Using a sample of $n = 50$ adults and a significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$, find the critical region for this test.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution
Since the alternative hypothesis is $H_a: p < 0.35$, small values of $X$ provide evidence in favor of $H_a$. Therefore, we are looking for a critical region in the lower tail of the binomial distribution. We use Rguroo’s Discrete Distributions Probability Calculator with the settings shown in  @fig-inactivity-rejection-dialog:

* Set the [No. of Trials]{.des} to [50]{.typein} and the [Prob. of Success]{.des} to [0.35]{.typein}, the boundary value of $p$ in $H_0$.
* From the dropdown, select [Lower Tail]{.dpd} and enter [$0.05$]{.typein} as the significance level $\alpha$.

Because we are using the inverse probability function, the calculator returns the boundary value of $X$ that leaves probability $0.05$ in the lower tail. We then use this value to determine the critical region.

```{r,echo=FALSE}
#| fig-alt: "Rguroo Discrete Distributions Probability Calculator configured for the Physical Inactivity example with Binomial distribution, 50 trials, probability of success 0.35, lower tail selected, and significance level 0.05 entered."
#| warning: FALSE
#| label: fig-inactivity-rejection-dialog
#| fig-cap: "Rguroo Probability Calculator Settings for the Physical Inactivity Critical Region Example"
#| out-width: "80%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_dialogs/Proportion_inference/inactive-rejection-dialog.png")
```

The output, shown in @fig-inactivity-rejection, gives
$$P(X \leq 12) = 0.06613 \geq 0.05 \quad \text{and} \quad 
P(X \leq 11) = 0.03423 \leq 0.05.$$

we reject $H_0$ in favor of $H_a: p < 0.35$.
```{r,echo=FALSE}
#| fig-alt: "Binomial distribution histogram for n = 50 and p = 0.35, with the critical region X less than or equal to 11 highlighted in gold, showing that P(X less than or equal to 12) = 0.06613 exceeds 0.05 and P(X less than or equal to 11) = 0.03423 does not."
#| warning: FALSE
#| label: fig-inactivity-rejection
#| fig-cap: "Rguroo Probability Calculator Output for the Physical Inactivity Critical Region Example"
#| out-width: "80%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/inactive_rejection.png")
```

This means that the decision rule $X \leq 12$ exceeds our significance level, 
while the decision rule $X \leq 11$ satisfies it. Therefore, the rejection 
region at significance level $\alpha = 0.05$ is 
$$X \leq 11.$$
That is, if we observe 11 or fewer inactive adults in our sample of $n = 50$, 
:::

::: {#exm-social-rejection-calc}
## Social Media as a Primary News Source: Finding the Critical Region

In the Social Media as a Primary News Source example 
(@exm-social-media-news-error), we are testing $H_0: p = 0.36$ versus 
$H_a: p \neq 0.36$, where $p$ is the true proportion of students who use 
social media as their primary news source. Using a sample of $n = 15$ students and a significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$, find the critical region for this test.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution

Since the alternative hypothesis is $H_a: p \neq 0.36$, both unusually small and unusually large values of $X$ provide evidence in favor of $H_a$. Therefore, we are looking for a two-sided critical region. For a two-sided test at significance level $\alpha = 0.05$, we split the significance level equally between the two tails, allocating $0.025$ to each tail so that the total Type I error probability is $0.05$.

We use Rguroo’s Discrete Distributions Probability Calculator with the settings shown in @fig-social-rejection-dialog:

* Set the [No. of Trials]{.des} to [15]{.typein} and the [Prob. of Success]{.des} to [0.36]{.typein}, the value of $p$ specified by $H_0$.
* From the dropdown, select [Outside Tails]{.dpd} and enter [$0.025$]{.typein} in each tail box.

Because we are using the inverse probability function, the calculator returns the boundary values of $X$ that leave probability $0.025$ in each tail. These boundaries determine the two-sided critical region.

```{r,echo=FALSE}
#| fig-alt: "Rguroo Discrete Distributions Probability Calculator configured for the Social Media example with Binomial distribution, 15 trials, probability of success 0.36, Outside Tails selected, and 0.025 entered in each tail."
#| warning: FALSE
#| label: fig-social-rejection-dialog
#| fig-cap: "Rguroo Probability Calculator Settings for the Social Media Critical Region Example"
#| out-width: "80%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_dialogs/Proportion_inference/social-rejection-dialog.png")
```

The output, shown in @fig-social-rejection, gives
$$P(X \leq 2) + P(X \geq 9) = 0.1032 \geq 0.05,$$
with the additional note that
$$P(X \leq 2) = 0.05281, \quad P(X \geq 9) = 0.05038,$$
$$P(X \leq 1) = 0.01168, \quad P(X \geq 10) = 0.01545.$$
```{r,echo=FALSE}
#| fig-alt: "Binomial distribution histogram for n = 15 and p = 0.36, with the critical region X less than or equal to 2 and X greater than or equal to 9 highlighted in gold, showing that P(X less than or equal to 2) plus P(X greater than or equal to 9) = 0.1032 exceeds 0.05, with additional tail probabilities noted."
#| warning: FALSE
#| label: fig-social-rejection
#| fig-cap: "Rguroo Probability Calculator Output for the Social Media Critical Region Example"
#| out-width: "80%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/social_rejection.png")
```

The decision rule $X \leq 2$ or $X \geq 9$ exceeds our 
significance level of $\alpha = 0.05$. Moving one step further in each tail, the decision rule $X \leq 1$ or $X \geq 10$ satisfies our significance level since 
$$P(X \leq 1) + P(X \geq 10) = 0.01168 + 0.01545 = 0.02713 \leq 0.05$$.
 Therefore, the critical region at significance level $\alpha = 0.05$ is $$X \leq 1 \quad \text{or} \quad X \geq 10.$$
That is, if we observe 1 or fewer, or 10 or more students in our sample of 
$n = 15$ who use social media as their primary news source, we reject $H_0$ 
in favor of $H_a: p \neq 0.36.$
:::


#### Using Probability Calculator to Compute the p-Value

We now illustrate how to compute the p-value and use it to make a decision, 
starting with the two one-sided examples that we have seen.

:::{#exm-youtube-pvalue-calc}
## YouTube Use: Computing the p-Value and Making a Decision

In the YouTube Use example (@exm-youtube-ppss), we are testing 
$H_0: p \leq 0.70$ versus $H_a: p > 0.70$, where $p$ is the true 
proportion of students in the district who use YouTube daily. A random sample of $n = 20$ students is selected and $x_{\text{obs}} = 17$ report daily YouTube use.

a. Obtain the $H_a$ support.
b. Compute the p-value.
c. At significance level $\alpha = 0.05$, make a decision and state your 
conclusion in the context of the problem.
:::

:::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution
a\. **Obtain the $H_a$ support.**

Since $H_a: p > 0.70$, values of $X$ that are at least as supportive of $H_a$ 
as $x_{\text{obs}} = 17$ are values greater than or equal to 17. Therefore the $H_a$ 
support is $\{17, 18, 19, 20\}$.

b\. **Compute the p-value.**

The p-value is computed at the boundary value $p_0 = 0.70$:
$$\text{p-value} = P(X \geq 17 \mid p = 0.70).$$

We compute this probability using Rguroo's Discrete Distributions Probability 
Calculator with $X \sim \text{Binomial}(20, 0.70)$.

@fig-youtube-pvalue-calc shows the Rguroo dialog and the output, giving

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
$$\text{p-value} = P(X \geq 17 \mid p = 0.70) \approx 0.1071.$$
:::

::: {#fig-youtube-pvalue-calc layout-ncol=2 layout-valign="top" fig-cap="Rguroo setup (left) and p-value output (right) for the YouTube example. "}

```{r,echo=FALSE}
#| fig-alt: "Rguroo Probability Calculator dialog configured for the YouTube p-value example with Binomial distribution, 20 trials, probability of success 0.70, and upper tail selected."
#| fig-cap: Rguroo dialog for computing the p-value
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_dialogs/Proportion_inference/youtube_pvalue_dialog.png")
```
```{r,echo=FALSE}
#| fig-alt: "Binomial distribution histogram for n = 20 and p = 0.70, with the p-value support highlighted, showing P(X greater than or equal to 17) = 0.1071."
#| fig-cap: "Rguroo output showing the p-value"
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/youtube_pvalue.png")
```
:::

c\. **Make a decision.**

Since the p-value $0.1071 > \alpha = 0.05$, we fail to reject $H_0$. The data 
do not provide sufficient evidence at the 5% significance level to conclude that 
more than 70% of students in the district use YouTube daily. Note that this 
conclusion is consistent with the critical region approach: $x_{\text{obs}} = 17$ 
does not fall in the critical region $X \geq 18$ determined in 
@exm-youtube-rejection-calc.

::::

:::{#exm-inactivity-pvalue-calc}
## Physical Inactivity: Computing the p-Value and Making a Decision

In the Physical Inactivity example (@exm-physical-inactivity-ppss), we are 
testing $H_0: p \geq 0.35$ versus $H_a: p < 0.35$, where $p$ is the 
true proportion of adults in the population who are physically inactive. A 
random sample of $n = 50$ adults is selected and $x_{\text{obs}} = 10$ are found to be physically inactive.

a. Obtain the $H_a$ support.
b. Compute the p-value.
c. At significance level $\alpha = 0.05$, make a decision and state your 
conclusion in the context of the problem.
:::

:::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution
a\. **Obtain the $H_a$ support.**

Since $H_a: p < 0.35$, values of $X$ that are at least as supportive of $H_a$ as $x_{\text{obs}} = 10$ are values less than or equal to 10. Therefore the $H_a$ support is $\{0, 1, \ldots, 10\}$.

b\. **Compute the p-value.**

The p-value is computed at the boundary value $p_0 = 0.35$:
$$\text{p-value} = P(X \leq 10 \mid p = 0.35).$$

We compute this probability using Rguroo's Discrete Probability 
Calculator with $X \sim \text{Binomial}(50, 0.35)$. @fig-inactivity-pvalue-calc shows the Rguroo dialog setup (left panel) and the Rguroo output (right panel) giving

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
$$\text{p-value} = P(X \leq 10 \mid p = 0.35) \approx 0.0160.$$
:::

::: {#fig-inactivity-pvalue-calc layout-ncol=2 layout-valign="bottom" fig-cap="Rguroo setup (left) and p-value output (right) for the Physical Inactivity example."}

```{r,echo=FALSE}
#| fig-alt: "Rguroo Probability Calculator dialog configured for the Physical Inactivity p-value example with Binomial distribution, 50 trials, probability of success 0.35, and lower tail selected."
#| fig-cap: "Rguroo dialog for computing the p-value"
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_dialogs/Proportion_inference/inactivity_pvalue_dialog.png")
```
```{r,echo=FALSE}
#| fig-alt: "Binomial distribution histogram for n = 50 and p = 0.35, with the p-value support highlighted, showing P(X less than or equal to 10)."
#| fig-cap: "Rguroo output showing the p-value"
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/inactivity_pvalue.png")
```
:::

c\. **Make a decision.**

Since the p-value $0.0160 < \alpha = 0.05$, we reject $H_0$ in favor of 
$H_a: p < 0.35$. The data provide sufficient evidence at the 5% significance 
level to conclude that fewer than 35% of adults in the population are physically 
inactive. Note that this conclusion is consistent with the critical region 
approach: $x_{\text{obs}} = 10$ falls in the critical region $X \leq 11$ determined 
in @exm-inactivity-rejection-calc.

::::

The two-sided case requires a bit more care. Since $H_a: p \neq p_0$ does not specify a direction, evidence against $H_0$ can come from either tail of the distribution. Recall from Case 3 that a value $x$ is in the $H_a$ support if $P(X = x \mid p = p_0) \leq P(X = x_{\text{obs}} \mid p = p_0)$, that is, if it is at least as unlikely as $x_{\text{obs}}$ under $H_0$.

:::{#exm-social-pvalue-calc}
## Social Media as a Primary News Source: Computing the p-Value and Making a Decision

In the Social Media as a Primary News Source example (@exm-social-media-news-ppss), we are testing $H_0: p = 0.36$ versus $H_a: p \neq 0.36$, where $p$ is the true proportion of students who use social media as their primary news source. A random sample of $n = 15$ students is selected and $x_{\text{obs}} = 9$ report using social media as their primary news source.

a. Obtain the $H_a$ support.
b. Compute the p-value.
c. At significance level $\alpha = 0.05$, make a decision and state your 
conclusion in the context of the problem.
:::

:::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution
a\. **Obtain the $H_a$ support.**

Since $H_a: p \neq 0.36$, values of $X$ that are at least as supportive of 
$H_a$ as the observed value $x_{\text{obs}} = 9$ are those that are at least as unlikely 
as $x_{\text{obs}} = 9$ under $H_0$. That is, the $H_a$ support consists of $x_{\text{obs}} = 9$ 
and all values $x$ for which
$$
P(X = x \mid p = 0.36) \leq P(X = 9 \mid p = 0.36).
$$

Figure @fig-social-pvalue-calc shows the Rguroo dialog and output used to compute 
$P(X = x \mid p = 0.36)$. The probability of the observed value is 
$P(X = 9 \mid p = 0.36) \approx 0.0349$. Therefore, any value of $x$ with 
probability less than or equal to $0.0349$ is included in the $H_a$ support, 
in addition to $x_{\text{obs}} = 9$.

From the graph, the $H_a$ support consists of $\{0, 1\}$ in the left tail and 
$\{9, 10, 11, \ldots, 15\}$ in the right tail.

Note that the graph is truncated at $X = 12$, since the probabilities for 
values greater than 12 are extremely small.

::: {#fig-social-pvalue-calc layout-ncol=2 layout-valign="bottom" fig-cap="Rguroo setup (left) and Rguroo output for $P(X=9)$ (right) for the Social Media example."}

```{r,echo=FALSE}
#| fig-alt: "Rguroo Probability Calculator dialog configured for the Social Media p-value example with Binomial distribution, 15 trials, probability of success 0.36, and probability of x = 9 computed."
#| fig-cap: 'Rguroo dialog'
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_dialogs/Proportion_inference/social_pvalue0_dialog.png")
```
```{r,echo=FALSE}
#| fig-alt: 'Binomial distribution histogram for n = 15 and p = 0.36,  showing the probabilty of $X = 9$'
#| fig-cap: 'Rguroo output'
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/social_pvalue0.png")
```
:::

b\. **Compute the p-value.**

The p-value is computed at the boundary value $p_0 = 0.36$. Using Rguroo’s 
Discrete Probability Calculator with $X \sim \text{Binomial}(15, 0.36)$, we 
compute the probability that $X$ falls in the $H_a$ support.

Recall that the $H_a$ support consists of the values $\{0, 1, 9, 10, 11, \ldots, 15\}$. 
Therefore, the p-value is the total probability of these values under $H_0$.

Figure @fig-social-pvalue-calc shows the Rguroo output, giving

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
$$
\text{p-value} = P\left(X \text{ is a value in the } H_a \text{ support} 
\mid p = 0.36\right) \approx 0.0621.
$$
:::

::: {#fig-social-pvalue-calc layout-ncol=2 layout-valign="bottom" fig-cap="Rguroo setup (left) and Rguroo output (right) for computing the p-value for the Social Media example."}

```{r,echo=FALSE}

#| fig-cap: 'Rguroo dialog'
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_dialogs/Proportion_inference/social_pvalue_dialog.png")
```

```{r,echo=FALSE}
#| fig-alt: 'Binomial distribution histogram for n = 15 and p = 0.36,  showing the p-value for the social media example$'

knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/social_pvalue.png")
```
:::

c\. **Make a decision.**

Since the p-value $0.0621 > \alpha = 0.05$, we fail to reject $H_0$ in favor of $H_a: p \neq 0.36$. The data do not provide sufficient evidence at the 5% significance level to conclude that the proportion of students who use social media as their primary news source differs from 0.36.

This conclusion is consistent with the critical region approach: the observed value $x_{\text{obs}} = 9$ does not fall in the critical region $X \leq 1$ or $X \geq 10$ determined in @exm-social-rejection-calc.

## Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion {#sec-confidence-interval-one-pop}

Recall from @sec-foundations-confidence-intervals that a confidence interval gives us a range of plausible values for a population parameter. In this section, our parameter is the population proportion $p$, and we use the sample proportion $\hat{p}$ as our estimate of it. Because $\hat{p}$ varies from sample to sample, we do not expect it to equal $p$ exactly. Instead, we use the observed sample proportion $\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}$ to construct an interval of plausible values for $p$.

As discussed in @sec-foundations-confidence-intervals, the confidence level describes the long-run success rate of the method used to construct the interval. For example, a 95% confidence interval comes from a method that captures the true value of $p$ in about 95% of repeated samples. In practice, however, we collect one sample and construct one interval.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
## Confidence Level
Imagine that we repeatedly take random samples from the same population and construct a confidence interval for $p$ using the same method each time. Because the samples differ, the intervals will also differ. Some intervals will contain the true population proportion $p$, while others will not.

The confidence level tells us the percentage of these intervals that we expect to contain the true value of $p$. For example, a 95% confidence level means that, over many repeated samples, about 95% of the intervals constructed using this method would contain the true population proportion $p$.
:::

Recall from @sec-foundations-confidence-intervals that we can construct a confidence interval by inverting a two-sided hypothesis test. For a population proportion, we consider different candidate values $p_0$ and test
$$
H_0:p=p_0
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
H_a:p\neq p_0.
$$
If we fail to reject $H_0$, our data are consistent with $p_0$, so we consider $p_0$ a plausible value for $p$. If we reject $H_0$, we do not consider $p_0$ plausible.  We repeat this process for different values of $p_0$. The collection of all values for which we fail to reject $H_0$ forms our confidence interval.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
## Confidence Interval by Test Inversion

A $(1-\alpha) \times 100\%$ confidence interval for $p$ consists of all candidate values $p_0$ for which we fail to reject

$$
H_0:p=p_0
$$

in a two-sided hypothesis test at significance level $\alpha$.
:::

The following example illustrates this idea by testing
a grid of values of $p_0$ and identifying which ones are consistent
with the observed data.

:::{#exm-youtube-ci-grid}
## Daily YouTube Use Among Teens: Building a Confidence Interval from a Grid

Recall @exm-youtube-ppss. A sample of $n = 20$ students produced
$x_{\text{obs}} = 17$ daily YouTube users, giving an observed sample proportion of
$\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 17/20 = 0.85$.

For each candidate value of $p_0$ shown in the grid below, carry out the two-sided
hypothesis test $H_0: p = p_0$ versus $H_a: p \neq p_0$ at
significance level $\alpha = 0.05$, using the binomial distribution with
$n = 20$ and $x_{\text{obs}} = 17$. Based on the results, identify the
range of values of $p_0$ for which we fail to reject $H_0$. 

```{r,echo=FALSE}
#| fig-alt: "A horizontal number line showing values from about 0.50 to 0.99 marked with evenly spaced dots. One value, 0.85, is highlighted with a diamond shape and labeled “p_obs = 0.85,” indicating the observed proportion among the possible values."
#| fig-cap: ""
#| out-width: "80%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/confidence_interval_grid_number_line_simple.svg")
```

:::


::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution

For each candidate value of $p_0$ in the grid, we compute the two-sided p-value
using the binomial distribution $X \sim \text{Binomial}(20, p_0)$. The
p-value is the probability of observing values of $X$ that are at least as supportive of $H_a$ as the observed value $x_{\text{obs}}=17$, assuming $H_0$ is true. We
then compare each p-value to $\alpha = 0.05$ to decide whether to reject
or fail to reject $H_0$.

| $p_0$ | p-value | Decision |
|---------|---------|----------|
| 0.55 | 0.006 | Reject $H_0$ |
| 0.60 | 0.022 | Reject $H_0$ |
| 0.65 | 0.064 | Fail to reject $H_0$ |
| 0.70 | 0.220 | Fail to reject $H_0$ |
| 0.75 | 0.439 | Fail to reject $H_0$ |
| 0.80 | 0.781 | Fail to reject $H_0$ |
| 0.85 | 1.000 | Fail to reject $H_0$ |
| 0.90 | 0.445 | Fail to reject $H_0$ |
| 0.95 | 0.075 | Fail to reject $H_0$ |
| 0.99 | 0.001 | Reject $H_0$ |

The graph below shows the result graphically:

```{r,echo=FALSE}
#| fig-alt: "A number line of possible proportion values with the observed value 0.85 highlighted. A central range is indicated as the “fail to reject” region, while values farther from the center fall into the critical regions."
#| fig-cap: ""
#| out-width: "80%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/confidence_interval_grid_number_line.svg")
```

As shown in the table and the graph, we fail to reject $H_0$ for candidate values of $p_0$
ranging from 0.65 to 0.95, and reject $H_0$ for the candidate values 0.55, 0.60 and 0.99. Based on this grid, the range of plausible values for $p$ is approximately $0.65$ to $0.95$.

This gives us an approximate 95% confidence interval based on the candidate values in our grid. If we tested more closely spaced values of $p_0$, we could locate the endpoints of the confidence interval more precisely.

:::

The confidence interval that we obtained in the example above is an approximation to
the collection of values of $p_0$$ that are consistent with our observed data at significance level $\alpha = 0.05$. Notice that the interval is not symmetric around
$\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.85$: it extends further below $\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}$
(down to approximately 0.65) than above it (up to approximately 0.95).
This asymmetry is not surprising when the sample proportion is close to 0 or 1. Recall the large-sample condition from @sec-large-sample-one-prop. Using $\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 0.85$ as our estimate of $p$, we compute:

$$
$$n\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 20 \times 0.85 = 17 \geq 10,
\; \text{but}\;
n(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}) = 20 \times 0.15 = 3 < 10.
$$

The large-sample condition fails because there are 3 observed failures. With a relatively small sample and a sample proportion close to 1, the binomial distribution can be noticeably skewed rather than approximately normal. As a result, an exact confidence interval need not be symmetric around $\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}$. A method based on a symmetric normal approximation may not work well in this situation.

This example illustrates that the choice of method for constructing a confidence interval matters. In the subsections that follow, we study two methods in detail. We begin in @sec-ci-large-sample with the large-sample method, which uses the normal approximation and produces a confidence interval that is symmetric around $\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}$. We consider this method first because it is widely used in practice and builds directly on the large-sample methods we have already developed for hypothesis testing. When the large-sample condition is satisfied, the normal approximation generally works well; however, it may be misleading when the condition is not satisfied, as in this example.

We then consider the exact binomial method in @sec-ci-binomial. This method does not rely on the normal approximation and can produce an asymmetric confidence interval. It is particularly useful when the large-sample condition is not satisfied.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Symmetry of the Normal-Approximation Interval

Because the normal distribution is symmetric, the large-sample confidence interval we will construct is symmetric around $\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}$. In contrast, an exact binomial confidence interval does not need to be symmetric. This difference can be especially noticeable when the sample size is small or $\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}$ is close to 0 or 1.
:::

### Confidence Interval Based on the Large Sample Normal Approximation {#sec-ci-large-sample}

We begin with the large-sample method for constructing a confidence interval for a population proportion. This method uses the normal approximation to the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$ and is one of the most commonly used methods for confidence intervals for a proportion. It also builds directly on the large-sample methods we used earlier for hypothesis testing.

Recall from @sec-large-sample-one-prop that when the large sample condition is satisfied, the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$ is approximately normal. We can use this normal distribution to determine how far we should extend on either side of the observed sample proportion $\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}$ to obtain a range of plausible values for $p$.

To construct the interval, we first need to estimate the variability of $\hat{p}$. Recall that the standard deviation of the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}$ is
$$\sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n}}.$$
Because the population proportion $p$ is unknown, we use the observed sample proportion $\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}$ in its place. The resulting estimate of the standard deviation is called the standard error of $\hat{p}$:
$$\text{SE}(\hat{p}) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}(1 - \hat{p}_{\text{obs}})}{n}}.$$

For a confidence interval, we check the large sample condition using $\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}$:
$$n\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \geq 10 \qquad \text{and} \qquad
n(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}) \geq 10.$$

When this condition is satisfied, the $(1-\alpha) \times 100\%$ 
confidence interval for $p$ takes the form

$$\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \pm z^* \times \text{SE}(\hat{p}),$$

where $z^*$ is the **critical value** from the standard normal
distribution corresponding to the desired confidence level. 

The quantity
$z^* \times \text{SE}(\hat{p})$ is called the **margin of error**. It tells us how far we extend below and above $\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}$ when constructing the interval. A larger margin of error produces a wider interval and reflects greater uncertainty in our estimate of $p$.

Common critical values are:

| Confidence Level | $\alpha$ | $z^*$ |
|-----------------|----------|-------|
| 90% | 0.10 | 1.645 |
| 95% | 0.05 | 1.960 |
| 99% | 0.01 | 2.576 |

::: {.callout-note}
## Large Sample Confidence Interval for a Population Proportion

When the large sample condition $n\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \geq 10$ and
$n(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}) \geq 10$ is satisfied, an approximate
$(1-\alpha) \times 100\%$ confidence interval for $p$ is:

$$\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} \pm \underbrace{z^* \times
\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}})}{n}}}_{\text{margin of error}},$$

which gives the interval

$$\left(\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} - z^* \times
\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}})}{n}},\;
\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} + z^* \times
\sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}})}{n}}\right).$$

This interval is always symmetric around $\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}$. When the large sample condition is satisfied, the normal approximation generally works well; when it is not, the resulting confidence interval may be misleading.
:::



:::{#exm-inactivity-ci-large-sample}
## Physical Inactivity Among Adults: Large Sample Confidence Interval

Recall @exm-physical-inactivity-ppss. A sample of $n = 50$ adults

for $p$, the true proportion of adults in the country who are physically
inactive. Interpret the interval.

b. Use Rguroo's [One-Population Proportion]{.fun} inference function
to obtain a 99% large sample normal approximation confidence interval
for $p$, and compare its width to the interval you obtained in part (a).

:::


::: {#solution-inactivity-ci-large-sample .callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution

a\. Click to expand the box below to see how to use the [Proportion Inference]{.fun}  function in Rguroo to obtain a large sample normal confidence interval for this problem.

1. Open the **Analytics** toolbox in Rguroo.

3. In the **Data** section of the dialog, enter the following:
   - In the [Factor Label]{.des} textbox, type a label for the categorical variable. In Rguroo, a “factor” refers to a categorical variable. For this example, enter [Physically Inactive]{.typein}.
   - In the [Success Label]{.des} textbox, type [Yes]{.typein}. A success corresponds to a person who is physically inactive.
   - In the [Failure Label]{.des} textbox, type [No]{.typein}.

b\. To obtain a 99% confidence interval, we use the same steps as in part (a) except for Step 4 of the Rguroo instructions, we enter [0.99]{.typein} instead of [0.95]{.typein} in the [Confidence Level]{.des} textbox.

The 99% confidence interval reported in the Rguroo output is $(0.0543, 0.3457)$ with width of 0.2914. This compares with the 95% confidence interval of $(0.0891, 0.3109)$ with a width of 0.2217. 

The 99% confidence interval is wider than the 95% confidence interval. For the same sample size and observed sample proportion, a higher confidence level produces a wider confidence interval. 
:::

As we saw in the example above, increasing the confidence level resulted in a wider confidence interval. This illustrates an important relationship between confidence level and interval width.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
## Confidence Level and Interval Width

For the same sample size and observed sample proportion, a higher confidence level produces a wider confidence interval. To be more confident that the interval captures the true population proportion, we must include a wider range of plausible values for $p$. This wider interval reflects the tradeoff we make to be more confident that the interval captures the true population proportion.
:::

:::{#exm-social-ci-large-sample}
## Social Media as a Primary News Source: Large Sample Confidence Interval

Recall @exm-social-media-pvalue-large-sample. A sample of $n = 35$ students
produced $x_{\text{obs}} = 21$ who reported using social media as their
primary news source, giving an observed sample proportion of
$\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 21/35 = 0.60$.

a. Check the 10-10 rule and determine whether the large sample normal approximation applies.


b. Use Rguroo's [One-Population Proportion]{.fun} inference function
to obtain a 95% large sample normal approximation confidence interval
for the true proportion of students at the university who get most of
their news from social media.

c. What is the margin of error for this interval?

d. In @exm-social-media-pvalue-large-sample, we tested the hypotheses
$$
\begin{cases}
H_0: p = 0.36 \\
H_a: p \neq 0.36.
\end{cases}
$$
Based on the confidence interval that you obtained in part (b), is $p=0.36$ a plausible value for the true proportion of students at the university who get most of their news from social media? How does your conclusion here compare to the conclusion from the hypothesis test in @exm-social-media-pvalue-large-sample?

:::

:::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution

a\. $$n\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 35 \times 0.6 = 21 \geq 10, \;
\text{and} \,
n(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}) = 35 \times 0.4 = 14 \geq 10.$$

Both quantities satisfy the 10-10 rule. Therefore, the large sample normal approximation is appropriate.

b\. The following is a screenshot of the [One Population Proportion Inference]{.dialog} dialog for obtaining the large sample normal confidence interval for this example.

```{r,echo=FALSE}
#| fig-alt: "Interface for one population proportion inference using a dataset on social media use. The sample size is 35 with 21 successes, giving a sample proportion of 0.60. The confidence interval section shows a 95% confidence level with the “Large Sample z” method selected, and no hypothesis test options are selected."
#| fig-cap: "Rguroo Basics dialog showing how to obtain large sample normal CI"
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_dialogs/Proportion_inference/normal-ci-social_dialog.png")
```
Click to expand the box below to see the Rguroo output.

::: {.callout-tip .inner-callout collapse="true" title="Rguroo output: One-Population Proportion Inference Output - Social Media"}

<div tabindex="0" class="rg-iframe-wrapper">
  <iframe
    src='Rguroo_html_output/Proportion Inference/socialNormalCI_docx/1_Population_Prop_3.html'
    class="rg-iframe"
    title="Rguroo output: One Population Proportion Large Sample Normal CI - Social Media Example">
  </iframe>
</div>

:::

From the Rguroo output, the 95% large sample confidence interval for
$p$ is $(0.4377, 0.7623)$. We are 95% confident that
the true proportion of students at the university who get most of
their news from social media is between 0.438 (43.8%) and 0.762 (76.2%).

c\. From the Rguroo output, the standard error is $0.0828079$. For a 95% confidence level, $z^*= 1.96$. Using these two values, 

$$\text{Margin of Error} = 0.0828079\times 1.96 \approx 0.1623$$
The Rguroo output also reports the width of the interval as $0.324601$. Using this value, you can also obtain the margin of error as
$$\text{Margin of Error}=\frac{\text{width of the interval}}{2} = \frac{0.324601}{2}\approx 0.1623.$$
d\. The interval $(0.4377, 0.7623)$ does not contain the null value of 0.36, so 0.36 is not a plausible value for $p$. This is consistent with the result of the hypothesis test in @exm-social-media-pvalue-large-sample, where we rejected the null hypothesis $H_0:p=0.36$.
::::

As we saw in @exm-social-ci-large-sample, the 95% confidence interval did not contain the null value $p_0=0.36$, and the corresponding two-sided hypothesis test at $\alpha=0.05$ rejected $H_0:p=0.36$. This is not a coincidence. Recall from @sec-foundations-confidence-intervals that a confidence interval can be constructed by inverting a two-sided hypothesis test.

More generally, a $(1-\alpha)\times100\%$ confidence interval and a two-sided hypothesis test at significance level $\alpha$ lead to the same decision. If the null value $p_0$ is inside the confidence interval, it is a plausible value for $p$ based on the observed data, and we fail to reject $H_0$. If $p_0$ is outside the confidence interval, it is not a plausible value for $p$, and we reject $H_0$.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
## Using a Confidence Interval to Make a Decision

For a two-sided hypothesis test
$$
H_0:p=p_0
\qquad\text{versus}\qquad
H_a:p\neq p_0,
$$ at significance level $\alpha$, use the corresponding $(1-\alpha)\times100%$ confidence interval:
If $p_0$ is inside the confidence interval, fail to reject $H_0$.
If $p_0$ is outside the confidence interval, reject $H_0$.
For example, a two-sided test at $\alpha=0.05$ corresponds to a 95% confidence interval.
:::

:::{#exm-gss-ci-large-sample}
## Marijuana Legalization: Large Sample Confidence Interval

Recall @exm-gss-marijuana-pvalue. The [GSS2024]{.data} dataset contains
responses from $n = 388$ U.S. adults, of whom $x_{\text{obs}} = 282$
supported the legalization of marijuana, giving a sample proportion of
$\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 282/388 \approx 0.7268$.

a. Check the 10-10 rule and determine whether the large sample normal approximation applies.

b. Use Rguroo's [One-Population Proportion]{.fun} inference function
to obtain a 95% large sample normal approximation confidence interval
for the true proportion of American adults who support the legalization
of marijuana.

c. What is the margin of error for this interval?

<div tabindex="0" style="width:85%; margin:auto;">

![Rguroo dataset logo](Rguroo_Icons/Rguroo_repo_logo.png) The dataset
for this example is available in the Rguroo dataset repository
[Kozak]{.repo}, with the dataset name [GSS2024]{.data}.

**Code book for Dataset GSS2024 is given [here](#code-book-gss2024).**

</div>

:::

::: {#solution-gss-ci-large-sample .callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution

a\. Checking the 10-10 rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
n\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}
&= 388 \times 0.7268 \approx 282 \geq 10, \\
n(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}})
&= 388 \times 0.2732 \approx 106 \geq 10.
\end{aligned}
$$
Both values satisfy the 10-10 rule. Therefore, the large sample normal approximation is appropriate.

### Confidence Interval Based on the Exact Binomial Method {#sec-ci-binomial}

As we saw in @exm-youtube-ci-grid, we can construct a confidence interval
for the population proportion $p$ by testing a grid of null hypotheses
$H_0: p = p_0$ and collecting all values of $p_0$ for which we fail
to reject $H_0$. When this approach uses the exact binomial distribution
to carry out each test, the resulting interval is called the **exact
binomial confidence interval**. As we noted in that example, this method
has an important advantage: it correctly reflects any asymmetry in the
data, which can occur when the large sample condition fails and the
binomial distribution is skewed.

Of course, testing every conceivable value of $p_0$ between 0 and 1
is not practical. Fortunately, efficient algorithms can locate the exact
endpoints of the interval directly, without testing each value one by
one. These algorithms are implemented in Rguroo, making it straightforward
to obtain the exact binomial confidence interval in practice. The
following example illustrates how.

:::{#exm-youtube-ci-binomial}
## Daily YouTube Use Among Teens: Exact Binomial Confidence Interval

Recall @exm-youtube-ppss. A sample of $n = 20$ students produced
$x_{\text{obs}} = 17$ daily YouTube users, giving a sample proportion of
$\hat{p}_{\text{obs}} = 17/20 = 0.85$. 

a. Use Rguroo's [One-Population Proportion]{.fun} inference function to construct a 95%
exact binomial confidence interval for the true proportion of students
in the district who use YouTube daily, and interpret the interval in the
context of the problem.

b. Check the 10-10 rule to determine whether we can use the large sample normal approximation for this problem?
:::

:::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution

a\. Click to expand the box below to see how to use the [Proportion Inference]{.fun}  function in Rguroo to obtain an exact binomial confidence interval for this problem.

::: {#prop-ci-binomial-youtube .callout-note appearance="simple" collapse="true" icon="none" title="![](Rguroo_Icons/R_circle_logo.svg){width=22px style='vertical-align:middle;'} Exact binomial confidence interval - YouTube example"}

1. Open the **Analytics** toolbox in Rguroo.  

2. From the [Analysis]{.dpd} dropdown, select [Proportion Inference]{.fun} → [One Population]{.fun}. This opens the [One Population Proportion Inference]{.dialog} dialog.

3. In the **Data** section of the dialog, enter the following:
   - In the [Factor Label]{.des} textbox, type a label for the categorical variable. In Rguroo, a “factor” refers to a categorical variable. For this example, enter [Daily YouTube Use]{.typein}.
   - In the [Success Label]{.des} textbox, type [Yes]{.typein}. A success corresponds to a student who uses YouTube daily.
   - In the [Failure Label]{.des} textbox, type [No]{.typein}.
   - In the [Sample Size]{.des} textbox, type [20]{.typein}.
   - In the [\# of Successes]{.des} textbox, type [17]{.typein}.

4. In the **Confidence Interval** section of the dialog, enter the following:
   - In the [Confidence Level]{.des} textbox, enter [0.95]{.typein}. This is the default value for a 95% confidence level.
   - Select the [Binomial (Exact)]{.des} checkbox to obtain the exact binomial confidence interval.

5. Click the preview icon ![preview icon](Rguroo_Icons/preview_inline.png) to view the output.

    src="Rguroo_html_output/Proportion Inference/YoutubeBinomCi_docx/YoutubeBinomCi.html"

From the Rguroo output, the 95% exact binomial confidence interval for
$p$ is $(0.628, 0.958)$. The following is an interpretation of this interval:

We are 95% confident that the true proportion of students in the district who use YouTube daily is between 0.628 (62.8%) and 0.958 (95.8%).

Notice that this interval is consistent with what we found using the grid in @exm-youtube-ci-grid, where we identified the range of plausible values as approximately 0.65 to 0.95. The exact interval extends the lower endpoint to 0.628, which lies between the grid values 0.60 and 0.65, where the p-value crossed the 0.05 threshold, just as we anticipated. The upper endpoint, 0.958, also agrees with the grid analysis, which placed the upper crossing between 0.95 (fail to reject) and 0.99 (reject). Thus, the grid approach gave us a good approximation to the range of plausible values, while the exact binomial method determines the endpoints more precisely.

b\. To check whether the large sample normal approximation is appropriate, we apply the 10-10 rule:
$$
\begin{aligned}
n\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}
&=20(0.85)=17\geq10,\\
n(1-\hat{p}_{\text{obs}})
&=20(0.15)=3<10.
\end{aligned}
$$
The second condition is not satisfied because there are only 3 observed failures. Therefore, the large sample normal approximation is not appropriate for this example.

Notice also that the exact binomial interval is not symmetric around $\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}=0.85$. Its midpoint, as reported in the Rguroo output, is approximately 0.793. Unlike the normal-approximation interval, the exact binomial interval does not need to be centered at the observed sample proportion.
::::
