## Hypothesis Testing for Two Proportions {#sec-hyp-test-two-prop}

Many important research questions require comparing proportions between two groups. In medical research, clinical trials compare treatment outcomes between patients receiving a new therapy and those receiving a placebo or standard care. In the social sciences, researchers investigate differences between demographic groups. In educational research, teachers evaluate whether new instructional methods outperform traditional approaches. Understanding how to compare two population proportions allows us to evaluate whether observed differences in sample data reflect genuine population differences or are due to chance variation.

Consider a few recent examples: A Phase 3 trial of the mRNA-1273 vaccine (Moderna) with over 30,000 participants found that 0.4% of the vaccinated group developed symptomatic COVID-19 compared to 4.9% in the placebo group—a substantial difference. A 2022 study examining 1,166 articles in *Political Psychology* found that 35.1% of lead authors were women compared to 64.9% men, highlighting a gender gap in academic publishing. In each case, researchers collected data from two independent samples, observed different sample proportions, and found statistical evidence that the population proportions differed.

While these large-scale studies demonstrate striking differences, many research questions involve smaller samples and more subtle effects where the statistical evidence is less clear-cut. In this section, we develop the concepts and tools for comparing two population proportions by working with examples where the answer is not immediately obvious and careful statistical reasoning is required.

We extend the hypothesis testing framework from one proportion to two proportions. The same core concepts—null and alternative hypotheses, test statistics, p-values, Type I and Type II errors, and significance levels—continue to apply. However, we now focus on the **difference between two population proportions** rather than a single proportion.

### The Null and Alternative Hypotheses

To develop these concepts and tools, we'll work with four examples: an educational intervention comparing instructional approaches for teaching proportional reasoning, a health behavior study evaluating text message reminders for medication adherence, a workplace wellness program assessing nicotine patches for smoking cessation, and an analysis of gender differences in attitudes toward marijuana legalization from the General Social Survey.

When comparing two population proportions, we focus on the difference between them. We have two populations—let's call one population 1 and the other population 2. It does not matter which population you designate as population 1 and which as population 2, as long as you clearly define your choice. We denote the population proportion for population 1 by $p_1$ and the population proportion for population 2 by $p_2$. Our goal is to make inferences about the difference between these proportions: $p_1 - p_2$. To do this, we begin by formulating hypotheses about this difference.

Just as in the one-population case, we can formulate both one-sided and two-sided tests. The three cases are:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Case 1: } 
&\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 \leq p_2 \\
H_a: p_1 > p_2
\end{cases}
\qquad
\text{Case 2: } 
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 \geq p_2 \\
H_a: p_1 < p_2
\end{cases} \\
\\
\text{Case 3: } 
&\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 = p_2 \\
H_a: p_1 \neq p_2
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
$$

We can equivalently write these hypotheses in terms of the difference $p_1 - p_2$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Case 1: } 
&\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 - p_2 \leq 0 \\
H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0
\end{cases}
\qquad
\text{Case 2: } 
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 - p_2 \geq 0 \\
H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0
\end{cases} \\
\\
\text{Case 3: } 
&\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0 \\
H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
$$

Cases 1 and 2 are one-sided tests, while Case 3 is a two-sided test. In practice, the choice of case depends on the research question—specifically, whether we are testing for an increase, a decrease, or any difference. Let's see how to set up the hypotheses for each of our examples.

:::{#exm-schema-hypotheses}
## Schema-Based Instruction: Stating Hypotheses

Researchers want to know whether a new schema-based instructional approach improves seventh-grade students' mastery of proportional reasoning compared to traditional instruction. They randomly assign 50 students to the new approach and 50 students to traditional instruction. Let $p_1$ represent the proportion of all students who would achieve mastery under the new approach, and $p_2$ represent the proportion who would achieve mastery under traditional instruction. State the appropriate null and alternative hypotheses to address the research question.
:::

:::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution

Since the researchers want to know whether the new approach *improves* mastery (that is, whether $p_1 > p_2$), this is a Case 1 situation. The hypotheses are:

$$
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 \leq p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_0: p_1 - p_2 \leq 0\\
H_a: p_1 > p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0
\end{cases}
$$

The null hypothesis states that the new approach is no better than (or is worse than) traditional instruction. The alternative hypothesis states that the new approach produces a higher mastery rate.
::::

:::{#exm-text-hypotheses}
## Text Message Reminders: Stating Hypotheses

Researchers are piloting a text message reminder system for diabetes patients. They want to know whether daily text reminders improve medication adherence compared to standard care, but they're also open to the possibility that the reminders might perform worse (perhaps by being annoying or overwhelming). They randomly assign 40 patients to receive text reminders and 50 patients to receive standard care. Let $p_1$ represent the proportion of all patients who would have good adherence with text reminders, and $p_2$ represent the proportion who would have good adherence with standard care. State the appropriate null and alternative hypotheses.
:::

:::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution

Since the researchers have no strong directional prediction and want to detect a difference in either direction, this is a Case 3 situation. The hypotheses are:

$$
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 = p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0\\
H_a: p_1 \neq p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0
\end{cases}
$$

The null hypothesis states that the difference between the two population proportions, $p_1$ and $p_2$, is zero. A difference of zero means that the two population proportions are equal, so there is no difference in adherence rates between the two approaches. The alternative hypothesis states that the difference is not zero, meaning that the adherence rates differ between the two approaches.
::::

:::{#exm-smoking-hypotheses}
## Smoking Cessation: Stating Hypotheses

A workplace wellness program is comparing two approaches to smoking cessation. Employees are randomly assigned to either receive free nicotine patches (60 employees - Group 1) or participate in a self-guided quitting program (60 employees - Group 2). However, the researchers believe that the self-guided approach might actually be more effective because it emphasizes personal commitment and doesn't rely on external aids. Let $p_1$ represent the proportion of all employees who would quit smoking with nicotine patches, and $p_2$ represent the proportion who would quit with the self-guided approach. State the appropriate null and alternative hypotheses to test whether the self-guided approach is more effective.
:::

:::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution

Since the researchers want to test whether the self-guided approach is *more effective* than nicotine patches (that is, whether $p_2 > p_1$, or equivalently $p_1 < p_2$), this is a Case 2 situation. The hypotheses are:

$$
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 \geq p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_0: p_1 - p_2 \geq 0\\
H_a: p_1 < p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0
\end{cases}
$$

The null hypothesis states that nicotine patches are at least as effective as (or more effective than) the self-guided approach. The alternative hypothesis states that the self-guided approach produces a higher quit rate.
::::

:::{#exm-gss-hypotheses}
## GSS 2024: Gender and Marijuana Legalization

The General Social Survey (GSS) is a long-running national survey that monitors societal change and studies the growing complexity of American society. In a representative sample from the GSS 2024 data, there are 204 females and 184 males who were asked whether they support the legalization of marijuana. Of the 204 females, 142 said they support legalization. Of the 184 males, 140 said they support legalization. Researchers want to know whether this sample provides evidence that the proportion of females who support legalization differs from the proportion of males who support legalization. Let $p_1$ represent the proportion of females in the population who support legalization, and $p_2$ represent the proportion of males who support legalization. State the appropriate null and alternative hypotheses.
:::

:::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution

Since the researchers want to know whether the proportions *differ* (in either direction) without specifying which gender should have higher support, this is a Case 3 situation. The hypotheses are:

$$
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 = p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0\\
H_a: p_1 \neq p_2 \quad \text{or equivalently} \quad H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0
\end{cases}
$$

The null hypothesis states that females and males support marijuana legalization at the same rate. The alternative hypothesis states that the support rates differ between the two groups.
::::

### Data, Statistic, and Sampling Distribution {#sec-data-stat-dist}

To make inferences about $p_1 - p_2$, we collect a sample of size $n_1$ from population 1 and a sample of size $n_2$ from population 2. Note that these sample sizes don't have to be equal—researchers often work with unequal group sizes due to practical constraints or deliberate design choices.

Let $X_1$ denote the number of successes (favorable outcomes) in our sample from population 1, and let $X_2$ denote the number of successes in our sample from population 2. Although we could compare the counts through $X_1-X_2$, differences in counts are difficult to analyze and can be misleading when the sample sizes differ. Instead, we compare sample proportions and rely on the Central Limit Theorem for large samples.


The sample proportions are $\hat{p}_1 = X_1/n_1$ and $\hat{p}_2 = X_2/n_2$. These are our point estimates of $p_1$ and $p_2$, respectively. To make inferences about the difference $p_1 - p_2$, we naturally use the difference in sample proportions: $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$.

**The Sampling Distribution of $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$**

When the sample sizes $n_1$ and $n_2$ are both sufficiently large, the Central Limit Theorem tells us that the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ is approximately normal. The rule of thumb for "sufficiently large" is that each group must have at least 10 successes and 10 failures: $n_1\hat{p}_1 \geq 10$, $n_1(1-\hat{p}_1) \geq 10$, $n_2\hat{p}_2 \geq 10$, and $n_2(1-\hat{p}_2) \geq 10$.

When these conditions are met, the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ is approximately normal with mean $p_1 - p_2$ and standard error

$$
\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \sim N\left(p_1 - p_2, \; \text{SE}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2)\right),
$$
where 
$$
\text{SE}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) = \sqrt{\frac{p_1(1-p_1)}{n_1} + \frac{p_2(1-p_2)}{n_2}}.
$$

Notice that the variability depends on both sample sizes and population proportions.

**Simplification Under the Null Hypothesis**

Recall that when testing hypotheses, we work at the boundary of the null hypothesis, since the Type I error is maximized there. For all three cases above, the boundary value is $p_1 - p_2 = 0$, which means $p_1 = p_2$.

At this boundary, the two population proportions are equal. We denote their common value by $p$, so that $p_1=p_2=p$. As a result, the standard error simplifies to:

$$
\text{SE}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2)
= \sqrt{\frac{p(1-p)}{n_1} + \frac{p(1-p)}{n_2}}
= \sqrt{p(1-p)\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}.
$$

Therefore, under the null hypothesis, the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ is:

$$
\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \sim N\left(0, \; \sqrt{p(1-p)\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}\right).
$$

This is the distribution we will use for hypothesis testing.

**Estimating the Common Proportion**

There is one practical issue: we do not know $p$, the common population proportion under $H_0$. Because $H_0$ assumes that $p_1=p_2$, we treat the two samples as coming from populations with the same proportion. We therefore combine the number of successes from both samples and divide by the combined sample size. This gives us an estimate of the common population proportion called the **pooled sample proportion**:
$$\hat{p} = \frac{X_1 + X_2}{n_1 + n_2}.$$

Using $\hat{p}$ in place of $p$ gives the **estimated standard error**:

$$
\widehat{\text{SE}}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) 
= \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}.
$$

This estimated standard error is used in our test statistic and in determining critical regions and p-values, just as we did in the one-population case.

The following example works through all of these computations for one of our four studies. The remaining three are summarized in @tbl-two-prop-summary.

:::{#exm-schema-quantities}
## Schema-Based Instruction: Computing the Key Quantities

In the schema-based instruction study, 50 students were assigned to the new approach and 50 to traditional instruction. After the intervention, 34 students in the new approach group achieved mastery, while 24 students in the traditional instruction group achieved mastery.

a. Compute the sample proportions $\hat{p}_1$ and $\hat{p}_2$ and their difference.
b. Verify the large sample conditions.
c. Compute the pooled sample proportion $\hat{p}$.
d. Compute the estimated standard error of $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$.
:::

:::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution

a\. **Sample proportions.**

$$\hat{p}_1 = \frac{34}{50} = 0.68, \qquad \hat{p}_2 = \frac{24}{50} = 0.48, \qquad \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 = 0.20.$$

The new approach shows a 20 percentage point higher mastery rate in the sample. We will test whether this provides sufficient evidence that $p_1 > p_2$ or whether it could reasonably arise by chance when both approaches are equally effective.

b\. **Large sample conditions.**

We check whether each group has at least 10 successes and 10 failures.

For Group 1 (new approach):

$$n_1 \hat{p}_1 = 50 \times 0.68 = 34, \qquad n_1(1 - \hat{p}_1) = 50 \times 0.32 = 16.$$

For Group 2 (traditional instruction):

$$n_2 \hat{p}_2 = 50 \times 0.48 = 24, \qquad n_2(1 - \hat{p}_2) = 50 \times 0.52 = 26.$$

All four counts are at least 10, so the large-sample conditions are satisfied and the Central Limit Theorem applies.

c\. **Pooled sample proportion.**

$$\hat{p} = \frac{34 + 24}{50 + 50} = \frac{58}{100} = 0.58.$$

Under the null hypothesis, we estimate that 58% of students would achieve mastery if both approaches were equally effective.

d\. **Estimated standard error.**

$$
\widehat{\text{SE}}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) 
= \sqrt{0.58 \times 0.42 \times \left(\frac{1}{50} + \frac{1}{50}\right)}
= \sqrt{0.009744}
\approx 0.0987.
$$

This is the typical sample-to-sample variability in $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ if the null hypothesis is true.
::::

The same computations for all four studies are summarized in @tbl-two-prop-summary. We will refer back to this table when working through hypothesis tests in the next subsection.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| label: tbl-two-prop-summary
#| tbl-cap: "Sample proportions, pooled proportion, large-sample check, and estimated standard error of $\\hat{p}_1 - \\hat{p}_2$ for the four studies. All four studies satisfy the large-sample conditions, since each group has at least 10 successes and 10 failures."

library(knitr)
df <- data.frame(
  Study  = c("Schema-Based Instruction", "Text Message Reminders",
             "Smoking Cessation", "GSS 2024 Marijuana Legalization"),
  n1     = c(50, 40, 60, 204),
  X1     = c(34, 32, 24, 142),
  n2     = c(50, 50, 60, 184),
  X2     = c(24, 28, 30, 140),
  p1hat  = c("0.680", "0.800", "0.400", "0.696"),
  p2hat  = c("0.480", "0.560", "0.500", "0.761"),
  diff   = c("0.200", "0.240", "$-0.100$", "$-0.065$"),
  phat   = c("0.580", "0.667", "0.450", "0.727"),
  SE     = c("0.0987", "0.1000", "0.0908", "0.0453")
)
colnames(df) <- c("Study",
                  "$n_1$", "$X_1$",
                  "$n_2$", "$X_2$",
                  "$\\hat{p}_1$", "$\\hat{p}_2$",
                  "$\\hat{p}_1 - \\hat{p}_2$",
                  "$\\hat{p}$",
                  "$\\widehat{\\text{SE}}$")
kable(df, align = "lrrrrrrrrr")
```

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Section Summary: Comparing Two Proportions

**Notation**

| Quantity | Population 1 | Population 2 |
|----------|--------------|--------------|
| Proportion (parameter) | $p_1$ | $p_2$ |
| Sample size | $n_1$ | $n_2$ |
| Number of successes | $X_1$ | $X_2$ |
| Proportion (statistic) | $\hat{p}_1 = X_1/n_1$ | $\hat{p}_2 = X_2/n_2$ |

The **pooled sample proportion**, used under $H_0: p_1 = p_2$, is
$$\hat{p} = \frac{X_1 + X_2}{n_1 + n_2}.$$

**Large Sample Conditions**

The normal approximation is appropriate when each sample has at least 10 successes and 10 failures:
$$n_1\hat{p}_1 \geq 10, \quad n_1(1-\hat{p}_1) \geq 10, \quad n_2\hat{p}_2 \geq 10, \quad n_2(1-\hat{p}_2) \geq 10.$$

**Null Distribution Under $H_0: p_1 = p_2$**

When $H_0$ is true and the large-sample conditions hold,
$$\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \sim N\left(0, \; \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}\right).$$

The **estimated standard error** is
$$\widehat{\text{SE}}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) = \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}.$$

This distribution and its standard error are used to compute critical regions and p-values for all three forms of $H_a$ (right-tailed, left-tailed, two-tailed).
:::

### Hypothesis Testing: p-Value and Critical Region Approaches

As we explained earlier, there are two equivalent approaches to making decisions in hypothesis testing: the p-value approach and the critical region approach. We now apply both approaches to testing hypotheses about the difference between two population proportions, $p_1-p_2$, and show how to carry them out using Rguroo.

Recall that we developed the sampling distribution of $\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2$ at the null boundary $p_1-p_2=0$ in the previous section. When the large-sample conditions are satisfied, we use this approximately normal distribution, together with the pooled sample proportion, to carry out the test. Both the p-value and critical region approaches use this same sampling distribution to determine whether the observed difference $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ provides sufficient evidence against $H_0$ and favors $H_a$.

::: {.callout-note}
## A Note on Notation

In the one-sample sections, we used $\hat{p}_{\text{obs}}$ to distinguish the observed sample proportion from the random variable $\hat{p}$. For two proportions, that notation becomes cumbersome — we would need $\hat{p}_{1,\text{obs}}$ and $\hat{p}_{2,\text{obs}}$. To keep the notation simpler, we use $\hat{p}_1$ and $\hat{p}_2$ for both meanings. The context will make the meaning clear: when discussing sampling distributions or probabilities, they represent random variables; when working with the observed data or making a decision, they represent the observed sample proportions.
:::

The p-value approach asks: "How much support does the observed difference provide for $H_a$?" The critical region approach asks: "Does the observed difference fall in the critical region?"  Both approaches lead to the same conclusion, and we will use Rguroo to carry out both approaches.

Let's examine each case in detail.

#### Case 1: Right-Tailed Test ($H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0$)

In this case, we want to test whether $p_1 > p_2$. The alternative hypothesis $H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0$ is supported when $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ is positive, with larger positive differences providing stronger support for $H_a$. Values near zero or negative provide little or no support for $H_a$.

**p-Value Approach:**

The p-value measures he strength of the evidence against $H_0$ and in favor of $H_a$. For a right-tailed test, the p-value is the probability of observing a difference that provides at least as much support for $H_a$ as our observed difference, assuming $p_1=p_2$:

$$\text{p-value}
=
P\left(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2
\geq \text{observed difference}\right),\;
\text{assuming } p_1=p_2.$$

This is the area to the right of the observed difference under the $N\left(0, \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}\right)$ distribution. A small p-value indicates strong evidence against $H_0$ and in favor of $H_a$, while a large p-value indicates that the data do not provide strong evidence against $H_0$.

**Decision Rule:**
- Reject $H_0$ if p-value $< \alpha$ (observed difference strongly support $H_a$)
- Fail to reject $H_0$ if p-value $\geq \alpha$ (data do not strongly support $H_a$)

**Critical Region Approach:**

The critical region consists of values in the upper tail of the sampling distribution. These are the values of $\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2$ that are sufficiently large to lead us to reject $H_0$ in favor of $H_a: p_1-p_2>0$. We find the critical value $c$ o that the probability of falling in the critical region is equal to the significant level $\alpha$, assuming $p_1=p_2$:

$$P\left(\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2 \geq c\right) = \alpha,\;
\text{assuming }p_1=p_2.$$

Using the sampling distribution under this assumption,

$$\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2\sim N\left(0, \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}\right)$$ 

we choose $c$ so that the area to the right of $c$ is $\alpha$. We reject $H_0$ if the observed difference $\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2$ falls in this critical region.

**Decision Rule:**
- Reject $H_0$ if $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 > c$ (observed difference strongly supports $H_a$)
- Fail to reject $H_0$ if $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c$ (observed difference does not strongly support $H_a$)

```{r, echo = FALSE}
#| label: fig-right-tail-critical-pvalue
#| fig-cap: "Critical region and p-value for a right-tailed test"
#| fig-alt: "Two side-by-side normal curves for the distribution of p-hat1 minus p-hat2. The left shows the upper-tail critical region beyond c, and the right shows the p-value area to the right of the observed difference. Both curves are centered at zero."

knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/right-tail-test.png")
```

:::{#exm-schema-test-pvalue}
## Schema-Based Instruction: Hypothesis Test - p-Value Example

For the schema-based instruction study, we want to test whether the new approach has a higher mastery rate than the traditional approach. Recall:

- $n_1 = 50$, $X_1 = 34$, $\hat{p}_1 = 0.68$
- $n_2 = 50$, $X_2 = 24$, $\hat{p}_2 = 0.48$
- $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 = 0.20$
- $\hat{p} = 0.58$

Hypotheses:
$$
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 - p_2 \leq 0\\
H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0.
\end{cases}
$$

a. Give a probability statement that describes the p-value.

b. Use Rguroo to obtain the p-value for the test and state your conclusion based on the significance level $\alpha = 0.05$.
:::


:::: {#schema-test-pvalue .callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution

a\. As discussed in @sec-data-stat-dist, assuming $p_1 = p_2$, the statistic $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ is approximately normally distributed with mean 0 and standard error 0.0987. The standard error is reported in the Rguroo output. Since $H_a:p_1-p_2>0$, differences that are at least as large as the observed difference of $0.20$ provide at least as much support for $H_a$. Therefore, the p-value is the probability of observing a difference of $0.20$ or greater,

$$
\text{p-value} = P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \geq 0.20), \; \text{assuming}\; p_1 = p_2.
$$
See @fig-pvalue-schema.

b\. **Using Rguroo**

Click to expand the box below to see how to use the [Proportion Inference]{.fun}  function in Rguroo to answer this question.

::: {#prop-inference-Schema .callout-note appearance="simple" collapse="true" icon="none" title="![](Rguroo_Icons/R_circle_logo.svg){width=22px style='vertical-align:middle;'} Two-Population Proportion Hypothesis Test: Schema-Based Instruction Example"}

1. Open the **Analytics** toolbox in Rguroo.  

2. From the [Analysis]{.dpd} dropdown, select [Proportion Inference]{.fun} → [Two Populations]{.fun}. This opens the [Two Population Proportion Inference]{.dialog} dialog.

3. In the **Response/Success** section of the dialog, enter the following:

   - In the [Response Label]{.des} textbox, type a label for the response variable. For this example, enter [Improves Mastery]{.typein}.
   - In the [Success Label]{.des} textbox, type [Yes]{.typein}. A success corresponds to a student improving mastery.
   - In the [Failure Label]{.des} textbox, type [No]{.typein}.

4. In the **Population** section of the dialog, enter the following:
   - In the [Population]{.des} textbox, enter a label for the population. In this example we enter [Seventh Graders]{.typein}.

5. In the [Data Summary]{.tab} tab, enter the sample information for populations 1 and 2.
   - In the **Population 1** section enter the following:
      - [Label]{.des}: [New]{.typein}
      - [Sample Size]{.des}: [50]{.typein}
      - [# of Successes]{.des}: [34]{.typein}
   - In the **Population 2** section enter the following:
      - [Label]{.des}: [Traditional]{.typein}
      - [Sample Size]{.des}: [50]{.typein}
      - [# of Successes]: [24]{.typein}

6. Click on the [Test of Hypothesis]{.tab} tab and specify the following:

   - From the dropdown next to [Alternative Hypothesis p1 - p2]{.des} select [>]{.typein}, the greater than sign, and in the corresponding textbox type in [0]{.typein}.
   - For [Significance Level]{.des} type in [0.05]{.typein}. This is the default value.
   - In the **Methods** section, select the [Large Sample z]{.des} checkbox.

7. Click the preview icon ![preview icon](Rguroo_Icons/preview_inline.png) to view the output.

8. Click the ![Save as](Rguroo_Icons/save_as.png) button and save the result as [SchemaProp2]{.typein}.

      - [Sample Size]{.des}: [50]{.typein}
      - [# of Successes]: [34]{.typein}
   - In the **Population 2** section enter the following:
      - [Label]{.des}: [Traditional]{.typein}
      - [Sample Size]{.des}: [50]{.typein}
      - [# of Successes]: [24]{.typein}

6. Click on the [Test of Hypothesis]{.tab} tab and specify the following:

   - From the dropdown next to [Alternative Hypothesis p1 - p2]{.des} select [>]{.typein}, the greater than sign, and in the corresponding textbox type in [0]{.typein}.
   - For [Significance Level]{.des} type [0.05]{.typein}. This is the default value.
   - In the **Methods** section, select the [Large Sample z]{.des} checkbox.

7. To obtain the critical region click the ![Details](Rguroo_Icons/details.png) button to open the [Advanced Features]{.dialog} dialog.
   - In the **Test of Hypothesis Graphs** section, select [Critical Region Graph]{.des}.
   - (Optional) Uncheck the [P-Value Graph]{.des}.

8. Click the preview icon ![preview icon](Rguroo_Icons/preview_inline.png) to view the output.

9. Click the ![Save as](Rguroo_Icons/save_as.png) button and save the result as [SchemaProp2cr]{.typein}.

Therefore, we reject $H_0$ at the significance level $\alpha=0.05$  and conclude that there is sufficient evidence in favor of $H_a: p_1 - p_2 > 0$. Thus, the data provide sufficient evidence that the mastery rate is higher for the new instructional approach than for the traditional approach.
::::


#### Case 2: Left-Tailed Test ($H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0$)

Case 2 is the mirror of Case 1. Small (negative) values of $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ support $H_a$, so the p-value and critical region lie in the **lower** tail of the null distribution.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**p-value:** $\quad \text{p-value} = P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq \text{observed difference} \mid p_1 = p_2)$

**Critical value $c$:** $\quad P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c \mid p_1 = p_2) = \alpha$

**Decision:** Reject $H_0$ if p-value $< \alpha$, equivalently if $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c$.
:::

```{r, echo = FALSE}
#| label: fig-left-tail-critical-pvalue
#| fig-cap: "Critical region and p-value for a left-tailed test"
#| fig-alt: "..."

knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/left-tail-test.png")
```

**Critical Region Approach:**

The critical region consists of values in the lower tail of the sampling distribution—these are the values that strongly support $H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0$. We find the critical value $c$ such that at the boundary where $p_1 = p_2$:

$$P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 < c \mid p_1 = p_2) = \alpha$$

Using the sampling distribution at the boundary, we find $c$ from $N\left(0, \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}\right)$ such that the area to the left equals $\alpha$.

**Decision Rule:**
- Reject $H_0$ if $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 < c$ (observed difference strongly supports $H_a$)
- Fail to reject $H_0$ if $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \geq c$ (observed difference does not strongly support $H_a$)

:::{#exm-smoking-test-pvalue}
## Smoking Cessation: Hypothesis Test - p-Value Example

For the smoking cessation study, we want to test whether the self-guided approach has a higher quit-smoking rate than the nicotine patch approach.  Recall:

- $n_1 = 60$, $X_1 = 24$, $\hat{p}_1 = 0.40$
- $n_2 = 60$, $X_2 = 30$, $\hat{p}_2 = 0.50$
- $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 = -0.10$

Hypotheses:
$$
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 - p_2 \geq 0\\
H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0.
\end{cases}
$$

a. Give a probability statement that describes the p-value.
b. Use Rguroo to obtain the p-value for the test and state your conclusion based on the significance level $\alpha = 0.10$.
:::

:::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution

a\. As discussed in @sec-data-stat-dist, assuming $p_1 = p_2$, the statistic $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ is approximately normally distributed with mean 0 and standard error 0.09083. Note that this standard error is reported in the Rguroo output.

The $p$-value is the probability of observing a difference at least as small as the observed difference of $-0.10$, assuming $p_1 = p_2$:
$$
\text{p-value} = P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq -0.10)\;\text{assuming}\;p_1 = p_2.
$$


b\. **Using Rguroo**

To perform this hypothesis test in Rguroo, follow the same steps given in the [solution](#schema-test-pvalue) of @exm-schema-test-pvalue. One difference is that in the [Test of Hypothesis]{.tab} tab, for [Alternative Hypothesis p1 − p2]{.des}, you should select the [<]{.typein} (less than) option because this is a left-tailed test, and set the [Significance Level]{.des} to 0.10. In addition, the values in the Basics dialog of [Two Population Proportion Inference]{.dialog} and in the [Data Summary]{.tab} tab should match those shown in @fig-smoking-inputs.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| fig-cap: "Rguroo input setup comparing quit-smoking success rates for nicotine patch and self-guided groups"
#| label: fig-smoking-inputs
#| fig-alt: "Screenshot of a Two Population Proportion Inference interface. The response variable is Quit Smoking with success defined as Yes and failure as No. The population variable is Treatment. Population 1 Nicotine Patch has a sample size of 60 with 24 successes proportion 0.4. Population 2 Self-Guided has a sample size of 60 with 30 successes proportion 0.5. Tabs for Data Summary, Confidence Interval, and Test of Hypothesis are visible."
knitr::include_graphics('Rguroo_dialogs/Proportion_inference/G_smoking_idialog.png')
```

Click to expand the box below to see the Rguroo output.

::: {.callout-tip .inner-callout collapse="true" title="Rguroo output: Two-Population Proportion Inference - Smoking Cessation Example"}

    src='Rguroo_html_output/Proportion Inference/smoking_prop2_pvalue_docx/smoking_prop2_pvalue.html'
    class="rg-iframe"

The p-value is depicted in the Rguroo output graph labeled **P-Value Graph: Large Sample z, Pooled SE** (shown in @fig-pvalue-smoke). In the left panel (labeled "Observed Data Scale"), the area corresponding to the $p$-value is shaded in red, and its value is 0.13546. This value is also reported in the results table.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "p-value for the Smoking Cessation study."
#| label: fig-pvalue-smoke
#| fig-alt: "Two side-by-side plots illustrating a left-tailed test using p-values. The left panel shows the observed data scale for the proportion difference Nicotine Patch minus Self-Guided with a normal curve centered at 0. The observed difference −0.1 is marked, and the left-tail area shaded in red represents the p-value of 0.13546. The right panel shows the standard normal z scale with the observed z statistic −1.101 marked. The left-tail area shaded in red represents the same p-value of 0.13546."
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics('Rguroo_html_output/Proportion Inference/smoking_prop2_pvalue_docx/G_pvalueTestPropz12.svg')
```

Since the p-value is $0.13546 > 0.10$, we fail to reject $H_0$ at the 10% significance level. There is not sufficient evidence in favor of  $H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0$.

Although the observed difference of $-0.10$ is in the direction of $H_a$  (the self-guided approach showed a 50% quit rate compared to 40% for nicotine patches), the p-value of 0.13546 indicates that a difference at least this supportive of $H_a$ is not particularly unusual, assuming $p_1=p_2$. Therefore, the data do not provide sufficient evidence that the self-guided approach has a higher quit-smoking rate than the nicotine patch approach.
::::

:::{#exm-smoking-test-cr}
## Smoking Cessation: Hypothesis Test - Critical Region Example

For the smoking cessation study, we want to test whether the self-guided approach has a higher quit-smoking rate than the nicotine patch approach. Recall:

- $n_1 = 60$, $X_1 = 24$, $\hat{p}_1 = 0.40$
- $n_2 = 60$, $X_2 = 30$, $\hat{p}_2 = 0.50$
- $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 = -0.10$

Hypotheses:
$$
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 - p_2 \geq 0\\
H_a: p_1 - p_2 < 0.
\end{cases}
$$

a. Using Rguroo, obtain the critical region for a test at significance level $\alpha =0.10$.
b. Based on the observed difference and the critical region in part (a), state the conclusion of the hypothesis test. 
:::

:::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution

a\. **Using Rguroo**

To perform this hypothesis test in Rguroo, follow the same steps given in the [solution](#exm-schema-test-cr) of @exm-schema-test-cr.  One difference is that in the [Test of Hypothesis]{.tab} tab, for [Alternative Hypothesis p1 − p2]{.des}, you should select the [<]{.typein} (less than) option because this is a left-tailed test, and set the [Significance Level]{.des} to [0.10]{.typein}. In addition, the values in the Basics dialog of [Two Population Proportion Inference]{.dialog} and in the [Data Summary]{.tab} tab should match those shown in @fig-smoking-inputs1.

Population 1 Nicotine Patch has a sample size of 60 with 24 successes proportion 0.4. Population 2 Self-Guided has a sample size of 60 with 30 successes proportion 0.5. Tabs for Data Summary, Confidence Interval, and Test of Hypothesis are visible."

:::

As discussed in @sec-data-stat-dist, assuming $p_1=p_2$, the statistic $\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2$ is approximately normally distributed with mean 0 and standard error 0.09083. We use this null distribution to determine the critical region.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "p-value for the Smoking Cessation study."
#| label: fig-cr-smoke
#| fig-alt: "Two side-by-side plots illustrating a left-tailed test using p-values. The left panel shows the observed data scale for the proportion difference Nicotine Patch minus Self-Guided with a normal curve centered at 0. The observed difference −0.1 is marked, and the left-tail area shaded in red represents the p-value of 0.13546. The right panel shows the standard normal z scale with the observed z statistic −1.101 marked. The left-tail area shaded in red represents the same p-value of 0.13546."
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics('Rguroo_html_output/Proportion Inference/smoking_prop2_cr_docx/G_crTestPropz12.svg')
```

From the Rguroo output graph labeled **Critical Region Graph: Large Sample z, Pooled SE** (shown in @fig-cr-smoke), the **critical value** is $c=-0.1164$, displayed at the bottom of the left panel. Therefore, the critical region is

$$
\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2<-0.1164.
$$


Since the observed difference $\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2=-0.10$ is greater than **$-0.1164$**, it does *not* fall in the critical region, as shown by the green triangle outside the red-shaded region. Therefore, we fail to reject $H_0$ at the **10%** significance level.


Although the observed difference of $-0.10$ is in the direction of $H_a$ (the self-guided approach had a 50% quit-smoking rate compared with 40% for the nicotine patch approach), the observed difference does not fall in the critical region. Therefore, the data do not provide sufficient evidence that the self-guided approach has a higher quit-smoking rate than the nicotine patch approach.
::::

#### Case 3: Two-Tailed Test ($H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0$)

In Case 3, $H_a$ is supported when $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ is far from zero in *either* direction. The p-value is therefore a *two-tail* probability, and the critical region occupies both tails with $\alpha/2$ in each.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
**p-value:** $\quad \text{p-value} = P(|\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2| \geq |\text{observed difference}| \mid p_1 = p_2)$

**Critical values $c_1, c_2$:** $\quad P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c_1 \mid p_1 = p_2) = P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \geq c_2 \mid p_1 = p_2) = \alpha/2$

**Decision:** Reject $H_0$ if p-value $< \alpha$, equivalently if $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c_1$ or $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \geq c_2$.
:::


```{r, echo = FALSE}
#| label: fig-two-tail-test-critical-pvalue
#| fig-cap: "Critical region and p-value for a two-tailed test"
#| fig-alt: "Two side-by-side normal curves centered at zero illustrating a two-tailed test. In the left panel, both tails are shaded to represent the critical regions, with each tail labeled $\alpha/2$ and dashed vertical lines at the negative and positive critical values. In the right panel, both tails beyond the observed statistic and its negative (labeled as observed) are shaded to represent the p-value, with dashed vertical lines marking these symmetric observed values."

knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/two-tail-test.png")
```

**Critical Region Approach:**

The critical region consists of values in both tails of the sampling distribution—these are the values that strongly support $H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0$. We find two critical values, $c_1$ and $c_2$, such that at the boundary where $p_1 = p_2$:

$$P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 < c_1 \text{ or } \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 > c_2 \mid p_1 = p_2) = \alpha$$

We split $\alpha$ equally between the two tails ($\alpha/2$ in each tail). Using the sampling distribution at the boundary:

- $c_1$ is the value with area $\alpha/2$ to its left
- $c_2$ is the value with area $\alpha/2$ to its right

**Decision Rule:**
- Reject $H_0$ if $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 < c_1$ or $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 > c_2$ (observed difference strongly supports $H_a$)
- Fail to reject $H_0$ if $c_1 \leq \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c_2$ (observed difference does not strongly support $H_a$)

:::{#exm-text-test-pvalue}
## Text Message Reminders: Hypothesis Test - p-Value Example

For the text message reminder study, we want to test whether adherence rates differ. Recall:

- $n_1 = 40$, $X_1 = 32$, $\hat{p}_1 = 0.80$
- $n_2 = 50$, $X_2 = 28$, $\hat{p}_2 = 0.56$
- $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 = 0.24$
- $\hat{p} = 0.667$

Hypotheses:
$$
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0\\
H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0
\end{cases}
$$

a. Give a probability statement that describes the p-value.

b. Use Rguroo to obtain the p-value for the test and state your conclusion based on the significance level $\alpha = 0.05$ .

:::

:::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution

a\. The $p$-value is the probability of observing an absolute difference at least as large as the observed difference of $0.24$, assuming $p_1 = p_2$:
$$
\text{p-value} = P(|\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2| \geq 0.24), \;\text{assuming}\;  p_1 = p_2.
$$
See @fig-pvalue-text.

b\. To perform this hypothesis test in Rguroo, follow the same steps given in the [solution](#schema-test-pvalue) of @exm-schema-test-pvalue. One difference is that in the [Test of Hypothesis]{.tab} tab, for [Alternative Hypothesis p1 − p2]{.des}, you should select the [!=]{.typein} (not equal to) option because this is a two-tailed test, and set the [Significance Level]{.des} to [0.05]{.typein}. In addition, the values in the Basics dialog of [Two Population Proportion Inference]{.dialog} and in the [Data Summary]{.tab} tab should match those shown in @fig-text-test-pvalue.

```{r, echo=FALSE}
#| fig-cap: "Rguroo input setup comparing success rates for text reminders and standard care"

The response variable is Medication Adherence with success defined as Yes and failure as No. The population variable is not yet selected. Population 1 Receive Text has a sample size of 40 with 32 successes proportion 0.8. Population 2 Standard care has a sample size of 50 with 28 successes proportion 0.56. Tabs for Data Summary, Confidence Interval, and Test of Hypothesis are visible."

Since this is a two-sided test, the 5% cutoff values $c_1$ and $c_2$ are determined so that 
$$
P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c_1 \text{ or }  \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \geq c_2) = 0.05, \; \text{assuming}\; p_1 = p_2.

From the Rguroo output graph labeled **Critical Region Graph: Large Sample z, Pooled SE** (shown in @fig-cr-text), these cutoff values are $c_1=-0.196$ and $c_2=0.196$, and are displayed at the bottom of the left panel labeled "Observed Data Scale". Therefore, the critical region is
$$
\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2 \leq -0.196
\qquad \text{or} \qquad
\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2 \geq 0.196.
$$
This means that observed differences falling in either tail are sufficiently extreme to lead us to reject $H_0$ at significance level $\alpha=0.05$.

```{r}

#| fig-alt: "Two side-by-side plots illustrating a two-tailed test at a 5% significance level. The left panel shows the observed data scale for the proportion difference Receive Text minus Standard care with a normal curve centered at 0 and red shaded critical regions in both tails. The critical values are −0.196 and 0.196. The observed difference 0.24 is marked and lies in the right critical region. The right panel shows the standard normal z scale with red shaded critical regions in both tails and critical values −1.96 and 1.96. The observed z statistic 2.4 is marked and lies in the right critical region."
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics('Rguroo_html_output/Proportion Inference/text_prop2_cr_docx/G_crTestPropz12.svg')
```

Since the observed difference $\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2=0.24>0.196$, it falls in the critical region, as shown by the green triangle inside the red-shaded region. Therefore, we reject $H_0$ at significance level $\alpha=0.05$ and conclude that there is sufficient evidence in favor of $H_a:p_1-p_2\neq0$.

The data therefore provide sufficient evidence that adherence rates differ between the two approaches. Since the observed adherence rate is higher for the text message reminder group (80%) than for the standard care group (56%), the results suggest that text message reminders are associated with higher adherence.
::::


So far, in the examples above, we have performed two-population proportion inference using summarized data—namely, the sample sizes and the number of successes for each group. In practice, however, we often begin with raw data rather than pre-computed summaries. By raw data, we mean datasets where each individual observation is recorded as a separate row, with variables indicating group membership and the outcome for each case. The following example demonstrates how we can carry out two-population proportion inference directly from raw data using Rguroo.

:::{#exm-gss-test}
## GSS 2024: Hypothesis Test Using Raw data

Consider the GSS marijuana legalization study. We want to test whether the proportion of U.S. adults who support the legalization of marijuana differs between females and males. Use the [GSS2024]{.data} to test the hypotheses:

$$
\begin{cases}
H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0\\
H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0,
\end{cases}
$$

where $p_1$ is the proportion of females who support legalization and $p_2$ is the proportion of males who support legalization. 

Using significance level $\alpha=0.05$, test these hypotheses using:

a. the p-value approach.
b. the critical region approach.

:::

:::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution

**Using Rguroo**

Click to expand the box below to see how to use the [Proportion Inference]{.fun}  function in Rguroo to answer this question.

::: {#prop2-inference-gss2024 .callout-note appearance="simple" collapse="true" icon="none" title="![](Rguroo_Icons/R_circle_logo.svg){width=22px style='vertical-align:middle;'} Two-Population proportion hypothesis test - Marijuana Legalization Example"}

**Before you begin:** Make sure you have already imported the [GSS2024]{.data} dataset into your Rguroo account, as shown [here](#Importing-GSS2024-to-Rguroo).

1. Open the **Analytics** toolbox in Rguroo.  
2. From the [Analysis]{.dpd} dropdown, select [Proportion Inference]{.fun} → [Two Populations]{.fun}. This opens the [Two Population Proportion Inference]{.dialog} dialog.
3. From the [Dataset]{.dpd} dropdown, select the dataset [GSS2024]{.data}.
4. Fill in the **Response/Success** section of the dialog as follows:

   - From the [Response]{.dpd} dropdown, select the factor [Grass]{.var}, the variable that indicates whether the respondents support legalization of marijuana.
   - From the [Success]{.dpd} dropdown, select the success level [Yes]{.typein}.
   - In the [Failure]{.dpd} textbox, enter [No]{.typein} (this is the default).
   - (Optional) In the [Response Label]{.des} textbox, enter [Legalize Marijuana]{.typein}. The label is usually a more descriptive version of the variable name.
5. In the **Population** section of the dialog, from the [Population]{.dpd} dropdown, select the variable [Sex]{.var}. You can optionally change the label for the population in the given textbox.
6. In the [Data Summary]{.tab} tab, select [Female]{.typein} from the [Level]{.dpd} dropdown for population 1, and [Male]{.typein} from the [Level]{.dpd} dropdown for population 2. Then click the refresh icon ![refresh icons](Rguroo_Icons/refresh_thin_Over.png) to display the summary statistics for each group.
7. Click the [Test of Hypothesis]{.tab} tab and enter the following:
   - In the [Alternative Hypothesis p1 - p2]{.dpd} dropdown, select [!=]{.typein} (not equal to) and enter [0]{.typein} in the textbox.
   - In the **Methods** section, select [Large Sample z]{.des}.
   - Leave the [Significance Level]{.des} textbox at the default value of [0.05]{.typein}.

(Optional) Click the ![Details](Rguroo_Icons/details.png) button to open the [Advanced Features]{.dialog} dialog, and in the **Test of Hypothesis Graph**, select both [P-Value]{.des} and [Critical Region]{.des}.     src="Rguroo_html_output/Proportion Inference/GSS2024Prop2_docx/GSS2024Prop2.html"

a\. p-Value Approach:**

The $p$-value measures the strength of evidence the data provide against $H_0$ and in favor of $H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0$. Because this is a two-sided test, differences at least as far from 0 as the observed difference of $-0.064791$, in either direction, are at least as supportive of $H_a$. Therefore, the p-value is
$$
\text{p-value}
=
P\left(|\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2|\geq0.064791\right),\;\text{assuming}\; p_1=p_2.
$$

This probability is shown in the Rguroo output graph labeled **P-Value Graph: Large Sample z, Pooled SE** (also shown in @fig-pvalue2-GSS). In the panel labeled "Observed Data Scale", the areas representing to the $p$-value are shaded in red, and the p-value is 0.15268. This value is also reported in the results table.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "p-value for the marijuana legalization example."
#| label: fig-pvalue2-GSS
#| fig-alt: "Plot titled Observed Data Scale showing a normal curve for the sampling distribution of the difference in proportions Female minus Male, centered at 0, with both tails shaded in red representing the p-value for a two-sided test, a green triangle marking the observed proportion difference of about −0.0648, and annotation indicating a p-value of approximately 0.1527."
#| out-width: "70%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/fig-pvalue2-GSS.png")
```

Since the p-value is $0.15268 > 0.05$, we fail to reject $H_0$ at significance level $\alpha = 0.05$. There is insufficient evidence in favor of $H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0$. Therefore, the data do not provide sufficient evidence that support for marijuana legalization differs between females and males.

b\. **Critical Region Approach:**

Since this is a two-sided test, the critical values values $c_1$ and $c_2$ are determined so that 
$$
P(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \leq c_1 \text{ or }  \hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 \geq c_2)= 0.05, \;\text{assuming}\; p_1 = p_2 .
$$

From the Rguroo output graph labeled **Critical Region Graph: Large Sample z, Pooled SE** (also shown in @fig-cr-GSS), these cutoff values are $c_1=-0.088794$ and $c_2=0.088794$. These values are displayed at the bottom of the panel labeled Observed Data Scale. Therefore, the critical region is
$$
\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2\leq-0.088794
\qquad\text{or}\qquad
\hat{p}_1-\hat{p}_2\geq0.088794.
$$
An observed difference that falls in either of these regions leads us to reject $H_0$ at significance level $\alpha=0.05$.

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Critical region for the marijuana legalization example, with $\alpha = 0.05$."
#| label: fig-cr-GSS
#| fig-alt: "Plot titled Observed Data Scale with significance level 5 percent showing a normal curve for the sampling distribution of the difference in proportions Female minus Male, centered at 0, with both tails shaded in red indicating the critical regions, a green triangle marking the observed proportion difference of about −0.0648, and labeled critical values at approximately −0.0888 and 0.0888."
#| out-width: "70%"
knitr::include_graphics("Rguroo_outputs/Proportion_Inference/fig-cr-GSS.png")
```

Since the observed difference $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2 = -0.064791$ lies between the two critical values, it does not fall in the critical region, as shown by the green triangle outside the red critical region. Therefore, we fail to reject $H_0$ at  significance level $\alpha = 0.05$ and conclude that there is **not** sufficient evidence in favor of $H_a: p_1 - p_2 \neq 0$.

**Conclusion:**

Both approaches lead to the same decision. At significance level $\alpha = 0.05$ , the data do not provide sufficient evidence that the proportion who support marijuana legalization differs between females and males.

### Homework for @sec-hyp-test-two-prop

For each of the following scenarios, complete these steps:

a. State the null and alternative hypotheses. In each case, clearly describe what the population proportions $p_1$ and $p_2$ represent in the context of the problem.

b. Calculate the observed sample proportions $\hat{p}_1$ and $\hat{p}_2$ and their difference $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$. Based on this observed difference, does the sample data appear consistent with the alternative hypothesis?

c. Compute the pooled sample proportion $\hat{p}$ and use it to obtain an estimate of the standard error of $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$.

d. Check whether the large sample test is valid by verifying that $n_1\hat{p} \geq 10$, $n_1(1-\hat{p}) \geq 10$, $n_2\hat{p} \geq 10$, and $n_2(1-\hat{p}) \geq 10$. If these conditions are not satisfied, stop here and note that the large sample test is not appropriate for this scenario and skip parts e, f, and g.

e. Use Rguroo to conduct the test of hypothesis using the critical region approach. Does the observed sample difference fall in the critical region? Based on this, do you reject $H_0$ at the 5% significance level?

f. Use Rguroo to obtain the $p$-value for the test of hypothesis. Is the $p$-value less than 0.05? Based on the $p$-value, do you reject $H_0$?

g. Write your conclusion in the context of the problem, stating what the results tell you about the scenario.

---

1. A researcher wants to determine whether male college students have a higher smoking rate than female college students. In a survey of 120 male students, 18 reported being regular smokers. Among 150 female students, 12 reported being regular smokers. Is there enough evidence to show that the proportion of male smokers is higher than the proportion of female smokers among college students? Test at the 5% level.

2. A school district is evaluating whether a new reading program is more effective for students with previous tutoring than for those without. Of 85 students with previous tutoring, 68 passed the reading assessment. Of 92 students without previous tutoring, 59 passed the assessment. Is there enough evidence to show that the proportion of students passing the assessment is higher for those with previous tutoring than for those without? Test at the 5% level.

3. A small clinic wants to compare the effectiveness of two different treatments for a skin condition. In a trial, 8 out of 25 patients receiving Treatment A showed improvement, while 12 out of 28 patients receiving Treatment B showed improvement. Is there enough evidence to show that the proportion of patients improving differs between the two treatments? Test at the 5% level.

4. A coffee shop owner wants to know if customer satisfaction is higher during the morning shift than the evening shift. Of 45 morning customers surveyed, 38 reported being satisfied with their service. Of 52 evening customers surveyed, 35 reported being satisfied. Is there enough evidence to show that the proportion of satisfied customers is higher in the morning than in the evening? Test at the 5% level.

5. Many high school students take the AP tests in different subject areas. In 2007, of the 211,693 students who took the calculus AB exam, 102,598 of them were female and 109,095 of them were male ("AP exam scores," 2013). Is there enough evidence to show that the proportion of female students taking the calculus AB exam is different from the proportion of male students taking the calculus AB exam? Test at the 5% level.

6. Are there more children diagnosed with Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) in states that have larger urban areas than in states that are mostly rural? In the state of Pennsylvania, a fairly urban state, there are 245 eight-year-olds diagnosed with ASD out of 18,440 eight-year-olds evaluated. In the state of Utah, a fairly rural state, there are 45 eight-year-olds diagnosed with ASD out of 2,123 eight-year-olds evaluated ("Autism and developmental," 2008). Is there enough evidence to show that the proportion of children diagnosed with ASD in Pennsylvania is higher than the proportion in Utah? Test at the 1% level.

7. A child dying from an accidental poisoning is a terrible incident. Is it more likely that a male child will get into poison than a female child? To find this out, data was collected that showed that out of 1,830 children between the ages of one and four who died from poisoning, 1,031 were males and 799 were females (Flanagan, Rooney & Griffiths, 2005). Do the data show that the proportion of male children dying of poisoning is higher than the proportion of female children? Test at the 1% level.

8. Many high school students take the AP tests in different subject areas. In 2007, of the 144,796 students who took the biology exam, 84,199 of them were female. In that same year, of the 211,693 students who took the calculus AB exam, 102,598 of them were female ("AP exam scores," 2013). Is there enough evidence to show that the proportion of female students taking the biology exam is different from the proportion of female students taking the calculus AB exam? Test at the 5% level.

9. The General Social Survey (GSS) collects data through different survey modes, including in-person interviews and telephone interviews. Researchers want to investigate whether the survey mode affects responses to sensitive questions. Using the GSS2024 dataset, test whether the proportion of respondents who support the legalization of marijuana differs between those surveyed in person and those surveyed by phone. The variable [Mode]{.var} indicates the survey mode (In Person or Phone), and the variable [Grass]{.var} indicates support for marijuana legalization (Yes or No). Test at the 5% level. **Note:** The `Mode` variable in the GSS2024 dataset includes three categories: In Person, Phone, and Web. When you select only the In Person and Phone groups in Rguroo for your analysis, Rguroo will automatically exclude respondents who completed the survey via the Web.

## Confidence Interval for the Difference Between Two Population Proportions {#sec-confidence-interval-two-prop}

In @sec-hyp-test-two-prop, we learned how to test whether two population proportions differ. For example, in the schema-based instruction study (@exm-schema-test-pvalue), we found strong evidence that the new instructional approach produced higher mastery rates than traditional instruction. The hypothesis test told us that a difference exists, but it didn't tell us how large that difference might be. Does the new approach improve mastery by 5 percentage points? 20 percentage points? 35 percentage points? The hypothesis test alone cannot answer this question.

This is where confidence intervals become valuable. A confidence interval for $p_1 - p_2$ provides a range of plausible values for the true difference between the two proportions, addressing the question "How large is the difference?" It tells us not just that a difference exists, but also gives us insight into the magnitude and direction of that difference. For instance, a confidence interval might tell us: "We are 95% confident that the new approach improves mastery rates by somewhere between 4 and 36 percentage points compared to traditional instruction." This additional information helps researchers, educators, and policymakers make more informed decisions.

Just as in the one-population case (@sec-confidence-interval-one-pop), a confidence interval for $p_1 - p_2$ can be derived by inverting hypothesis tests: given the observed difference $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$, the $(1-\alpha) \times 100\%$ interval consists of all values $d$ for which we would fail to reject $H_0: p_1 - p_2 = d$ in a two-sided test at significance level $\alpha$. And as in the one-population case, the **confidence level** describes the long-run behavior of the construction method, not any single interval — a 95% method captures the true difference in 95% of repeated samples. In practice we use a direct formula based on the normal approximation rather than carrying out the test inversion by hand, but the logic is the same.


### Large Sample Confidence Interval for $p_1 - p_2$ {#sec-ci-two-prop-large-sample}

When the large sample conditions are satisfied, we can construct a confidence interval for $p_1 - p_2$ using the normal approximation. Recall from @sec-data-stat-dist that when both samples are sufficiently large, the difference in sample proportions $\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2$ follows an approximately normal distribution.

However, there is an important difference between constructing a confidence interval and conducting a hypothesis test. In hypothesis testing, we assumed $H_0: p_1 = p_2$ was true, which allowed us to use a pooled estimate $\hat{p}$ for the common proportion. When constructing a confidence interval, we do not assume the proportions are equal—in fact, we're trying to estimate how different they are! Therefore, we cannot use the pooled proportion.

Instead, for a confidence interval, we estimate the standard error using the individual sample proportions $\hat{p}_1$ and $\hat{p}_2$:

$$\text{SE}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}.$$

This is called the **unpooled standard error**, or simply the **standard error**, because we do not pool the two samples together.

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal"}
## Pooled vs. Unpooled Standard Error

The two-proportion confidence interval uses the **unpooled** standard error, based on $\hat{p}_1$ and $\hat{p}_2$ separately:
$$\text{SE}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) = \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}.$$

The two-proportion **hypothesis test**, by contrast, uses the **pooled** standard error, based on the common proportion $\hat{p}$ under $H_0: p_1 = p_2$ (see @sec-data-stat-dist):
$$\widehat{\text{SE}}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) = \sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})\left(\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}\right)}.$$

The reason is the assumption being made. The hypothesis test assumes $p_1 = p_2$, so we pool. The confidence interval makes no such assumption — we're trying to estimate the difference, not assume it away — so we estimate each proportion's variance from its own sample.
:::

The large sample conditions for a confidence interval are the same as those for hypothesis testing. We need at least 10 successes and at least 10 failures in each group:

$$n_1\hat{p}_1 \geq 10, \quad n_1(1-\hat{p}_1) \geq 10, \quad n_2\hat{p}_2 \geq 10, \quad n_2(1-\hat{p}_2) \geq 10.$$

When these conditions are satisfied, the $(1-\alpha) \times 100\%$ confidence interval for $p_1 - p_2$ takes the form:

$$(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) \pm z^* \times \text{SE}(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2),$$

where $z^*$ is the critical value from the standard normal distribution corresponding to the desired confidence level, just as in the one-population case.

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Large Sample Confidence Interval for $p_1 - p_2$

When the large sample conditions are satisfied, an approximate $(1-\alpha) \times 100\%$ confidence interval for $p_1 - p_2$ is:

$$(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) \pm \underbrace{z^* \times \sqrt{\frac{\hat{p}_1(1-\hat{p}_1)}{n_1} + \frac{\hat{p}_2(1-\hat{p}_2)}{n_2}}}_{\text{margin of error}}.$$

That is, the lower endpoint is $(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) - z^* \cdot \text{SE}$ and the upper endpoint is $(\hat{p}_1 - \hat{p}_2) + z^* \cdot \text{SE}$, where $\text{SE}$ is the unpooled standard error given above.
:::

Common critical values remain the same:

| Confidence Level | $\alpha$ | $z^*$ |
|-----------------|----------|-------|
| 90% | 0.10 | 1.645 |
| 95% | 0.05 | 1.960 |
| 99% | 0.01 | 2.576 |

Let's see how to construct and interpret confidence intervals for the difference between two proportions using our earlier examples.



### Relationship Between Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Tests

There is an important connection between confidence intervals and two-sided hypothesis tests. A $(1-\alpha)\times100%$ confidence interval and a two-sided hypothesis test at significance level $\alpha$ lead to the same conclusion about the null value $p_1-p_2=0$:

- If a $(1-\alpha) \times 100\%$ confidence interval for $p_1 - p_2$ **does not contain 0**, then 0 is not a plausible value for $p_1-p_2$, and we **reject** $H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0$ at significance level $\alpha$ in a two-sided test.

- If a $(1-\alpha) \times 100\%$ confidence interval for $p_1 - p_2$ **contains 0**, 0 is a plausible value for $p_1-p_2$, and we **fail to reject** $H_0: p_1 - p_2 = 0$ at significance level $\alpha$ in a two-sided test.

This relationship provides a quick way to connect the confidence interval to the corresponding two-sided hypothesis test. As noted, however, confidence intervals provide more information than hypothesis tests alone. They tell us not just whether the data provide evidence of a difference, but also which values are plausible for the size and direction of the difference.

This direct relationship applies only to two-sided hypothesis tests. For a one-sided hypothesis test, you should not use this confidence interval rule to determine whether to reject $H_0$.

:::{#exm-schema-ci}
## Schema-Based Instruction: Confidence Interval

Recall @exm-schema-test-pvalue. In the schema-based instruction study, 50 students were assigned to the new approach and 50 to traditional instruction. After the intervention, 34 students in the new approach group achieved mastery ($\hat{p}_1 = 0.68$), while 24 students in the traditional instruction group achieved mastery ($\hat{p}_2 = 0.48$).

a. Check whether the large sample conditions are satisfied for constructing a confidence interval.
b. Use Rguroo's [Two-Population Proportion]{.fun} inference function to construct a 95% confidence interval for the true difference in mastery rates between the two approaches, and interpret the interval in the context of the problem.
:::

:::: {.callout-tip .solution-callout collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🔎 Solution

a\. We check the large sample conditions using the individual sample proportions:

   - Group 1 (new approach): $n_1\hat{p}_1 = 50 \times 0.68 = 34 \geq 10$ and $n_1(1-\hat{p}_1) = 50 \times 0.32 = 16 \geq 10$
   - Group 2 (traditional): $n_2\hat{p}_2 = 50 \times 0.48 = 24 \geq 10$ and $n_2(1-\hat{p}_2) = 50 \times 0.52 = 26 \geq 10$

All four conditions are satisfied, so the large-sample normal approximation is appropriate for constructing the confidence interval.

b\. Click to expand the box below to see how to use the [Proportion Inference]{.fun} function in Rguroo to obtain a large sample confidence interval for this problem.

::: {#prop-ci-two-prop-schema .callout-note appearance="simple" collapse="true" icon="none" title="![](Rguroo_Icons/R_circle_logo.svg){width=22px style='vertical-align:middle;'} Two-population large sample confidence interval - Schema example"}

1. Open the **Analytics** toolbox in Rguroo.  

2. From the [Analysis]{.dpd} dropdown, select [Proportion Inference]{.fun} → [Two Populations]{.fun}. This opens the [Two Population Proportion Inference]{.dialog} dialog.

3. In the **Response/Success** section of the dialog, enter the same information as in @exm-schema-test-pvalue:
   - [Response Label]{.des}: [Improves Mastery]{.typein}
   - [Success Label]{.des}: [Yes]{.typein}
   - [Failure Label]{.des}: [No]{.typein}

4. In the **Population** section, enter [Seventh Graders]{.typein}.

5. In the [Data Summary]{.tab} tab, enter the data for both populations:
   - **Population 1**: [Label]{.des}: [New]{.typein}, [Sample Size]{.des}: [50]{.typein}, [# of Successes]{.des}: [34]{.typein}
   - **Population 2**: [Label]{.des}: [Traditional]{.typein}, [Sample Size]{.des}: [50]{.typein}, [# of Successes]{.des}: [24]{.typein}

6. Click on the [Confidence Interval]{.tab} tab and specify the following:
   - In the [Confidence Level]{.des} textbox, enter [0.95]{.typein}. This is the default value corresponding to 95% confidence.
   - In the **Methods** section, select the checkbox [Large Sample z]{.des}.

7. Click the preview icon ![preview icon](Rguroo_Icons/preview_inline.png) to view the output.

8. Click the ![Save as](Rguroo_Icons/save_as.png) button and save the result as [SchemaCI]{.typein}.
